This document exists to reset the project on a cleaner intellectual basis, not merely to continue prior momentum.

The research is being restarted because the project has accumulated multiple layers at once:

  • an original conceptual framing,

  • later deep-research expansions,

  • a first-pass implemented repository,

  • a governance layer that now imposes stricter truth, contradiction, and comparability discipline,

The goal of this document is therefore not to pick a flashy final architecture. The goal is to establish a restart-grade foundation that is:

  • academically defensible,

  • hard on weak ideas,

This document also exists because your current repository appears stronger at the engineering layer than the project was earlier, but that does not automatically mean the scientific framing is equally mature. That mismatch matters. A repository can be modular, tested, and well-structured while still pursuing the wrong target, the wrong benchmark emphasis, or an overcomplicated set of modalities. Repository strength and thesis strength are not the same thing. Twelve Data+2arXiv+2

This restart is therefore justified by four realities:

  • The project’s strongest idea is still intellectually valid: model a changing information state rather than pretend that each article has a clean isolated causal effect.

  • The repository has grown into a coherent first-pass research system with adjusted-price handling, market features, labels, event-state aggregation, walk-forward validation, purge/embargo logic, and baseline plus first multimodal training support.

  • Several extension ideas are now competing for attention, and many of them are not equally defensible, equally modular, or equally benchmark-clean.

  • Your new derivative proposal is exactly the kind of idea that can look elegant while being low incremental value, noisy, redundant, or scientifically distracting unless examined critically.

This restart document is therefore a map for understanding first and choosing later.

  1. Governance basis and epistemic rules for the restart

The Agent governance documents materially change how this research should now be conducted.

The foundational rule is a declared truth chain:
Theory -> Design -> Code -> Tests and Benchmarks -> Update and Retraining Operations.
That is not decorative language. It means the thesis question must govern the architecture, the architecture must govern the implementation, and benchmark outcomes are not allowed to silently redefine the thesis objective after the fact.

The most important epistemic consequences are these:

  • If a capability is not shown in the repository materials, it must be treated as not established.

  • If a path seems likely but is not proved, it must stay provisional.

  • If a provider behavior, benchmark assumption, or implementation status depends on live reality, plan details, or runtime conditions, it must remain explicitly uncertain until manually verified.

  • Contradictions are not to be smoothed over. They are to be surfaced, resolved by authority hierarchy, and recorded.

  • Benchmark comparability is not a soft concern. It is treated as a tracked governance object with explicit states such as fully comparable, partially comparable, not comparable, or invalidated.

That governance layer matters to this restart because financial ML is especially vulnerable to attractive self-deception:

  • “The new model is better” when the label changed.

  • “The benchmark improved” when the universe changed.

  • “The architecture is stronger” when alignment changed.

  • “The richer feature family helps” when the split logic or leakage control changed.

  • “The result is stable” when only one recent holdout was viewed.

The current governance documents push against exactly that failure mode by forcing explicit handling of:

  • uncertainty,

  • contradiction,

  • evidence,

  • drift,

  • and comparability.

This is a major improvement over casual project continuation.

The practical epistemic rules for the restart should therefore be:

  • Established from repository evidence:
    The project is an end-of-day, multimodal, multi-horizon forecasting system, not a trading bot, not intraday, and not a raw price-level predictor. The repository documents repeatedly define it that way.

  • Supported by external literature or official documentation:
    Time-aware evaluation, purge/embargo logic for overlapping-label settings, proper scoring and ranking metrics, return-based targets, and multimodal fusion concerns are well grounded in the literature and official references. arXiv+3mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu+3mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu+3

  • Plausible but unverified:
    Some “implemented” claims in repository-facing documents may be declaratively true but still require runtime confirmation under real providers, live quotas, and real historical completeness. The implementation roadmap itself still flags manual external verification as unfinished.

  • Uncertain, verify manually:
    Live provider behavior, full historical completeness, split-event source sufficiency on the active plan, and final real-data runtime stability.

The governance consequence is simple:
The restarted research should prefer fewer, cleaner, benchmark-comparable claims over more ambitious but less falsifiable ones.

  1. Reconstruction of the project’s original intent and evolution

4.1 Original intent

The HTML project origin material and early research design are very clear on the original intention.

The project began as:

  • limited to 30 to 100 liquid large-cap stocks,

  • multi-horizon at 1, 5, 20, and optionally 60 trading days,

  • comparing market-only baselines against a multimodal model using market features plus a news-derived event state,

  • explicitly rejecting direct raw price-level prediction,

  • explicitly rejecting the assumption that one article cleanly maps to one isolated price effect.

That original framing is still the project’s strongest conceptual core.

  • Multi-horizon prediction.

  • Leakage awareness.

  • Walk-forward or temporally clean evaluation.

  • Split handling as a major scientific blocker.

  • Baselines first, multimodal second, richer architectures later.

These stable elements should be treated as the real spine of the research.

  1. Current project identity

5.1 What the project is

The project is best defined as:
an end-of-day, multimodal, multi-horizon, leakage-aware financial forecasting thesis project that tests whether a temporally aggregated event-state derived from news adds predictive value beyond market-only features for horizon-specific stock outcomes.

5.2 What the project is not

It is not:

  • a direct price predictor,

  • a trading bot,

  • an intraday or HFT system,

  • a clean causal event study,

  • a pure NLP project,

  • a pure tabular-alpha project,

  • a portfolio execution thesis.

5.3 Strongest academic framing

The strongest academic framing is not “financial news impact prediction” in the naive sense.

That phrase is risky because it can sound like clean causal attribution from article to price.

A stronger framing is:

Temporal multimodal forecasting of horizon-specific stock outcomes using a leakage-safe event-state representation of recent firm-related news.

That framing is stronger because it:

  • preserves the central insight,

  • avoids overclaiming causal isolation,

  • aligns with the repository’s event-state stance,

  • keeps the thesis predictive rather than causally inflated,

  • and supports fair comparison against market-only baselines.

5.4 Best core thesis claim, at this stage

The thesis should most likely aim to show:

Under strict end-of-day alignment, split-safe labels, and walk-forward purged evaluation, a recency-weighted event-state representation of recent firm news provides measurable incremental predictive value over conservative market-only baselines for selected forecast horizons.

That is much stronger than:
“news predicts stocks”
and much safer than:
“our multimodal architecture beats the state of the art.”

  1. Core theoretical concepts

6.1 Event state

Event state is the latent, evolving information condition implied by recent relevant news for a firm as of date t.

It is not one headline.
It is not one sentiment score.
It is not clean causal identification.

It is an aggregated representation of recent, overlapping, partially redundant, partially conflicting information arriving through time.

This concept is theoretically justified because financial news is overlapping, persistent, confounded, and narrative-driven. Treating it as an information state is more realistic than pretending article-level isolation is scientifically clean. Ding et al. style event-driven prediction supports the relevance of event representation, while the project’s stronger stance is to aggregate rather than atomize. ijcai.org+1

6.2 Multimodality

Multimodality here means at least:

  • numeric EOD market inputs,

  • timestamped text-derived event-state inputs,

  • optional static or slow-moving firm context.

The challenge is not merely concatenation. The challenge is asynchronous alignment, different noise properties, and different horizon relevance. Broader multimodal time-series work emphasizes misalignment, heterogeneity, and modality-specific noise as central problems. arXiv+1

6.3 Multi-horizon forecasting

Multi-horizon forecasting means separate future outcomes for 1, 5, 20, and possibly 60 trading days, not merely one target stretched across time.

That matters because:

  • 1 day is closer to immediate reaction and noise,

  • 5 days is short-run absorption or drift,

  • 20 days is medium-horizon repricing,

  • 60 days is slower narrative or profile effect.

The project should not expect one feature family to help equally across all horizons.

6.4 Market-only baseline

The market-only baseline is not a bureaucratic requirement. It is the scientific reference class.

Without a strong market-only baseline, the project cannot tell whether:

  • news helps,

  • features are redundant,

  • the multimodal model is merely over-parameterized,

  • or leakage is being mistaken for signal.

6.5 Company, profile, or context information

This is a support family, not obviously a core family.

Static identity metadata can help:

  • entity linking,

  • ticker reconciliation,

  • cross-sectional priors,

  • cold-start support.

Time-varying descriptive profile information is much riskier because it can easily leak future knowledge into past predictions if not point-in-time indexed.

6.6 Ranking versus regression versus risk prediction

These are not interchangeable.

Regression asks:
Can you estimate numeric future outcomes?

Ranking asks:
Can you order names cross-sectionally by future relative performance?

Risk prediction asks:
Can you estimate downside, uncertainty, or tail sensitivity?

For this project, ranking may be more decision-relevant than raw point prediction in some settings, but regression on excess or abnormal returns remains a stronger foundational primary target because it is closer to the project’s original scientific question and easier to stage cleanly. Proper ranking metrics and probabilistic scoring rules should remain in the benchmark map, not necessarily as the only primary objective. ideas.repec.org+2sites.stat.washington.edu+2

6.7 Temporal alignment

Temporal alignment means every input used for date t must have been available by the chosen cutoff for date t.

In this project that means:

  • market data as of EOD t,

  • only news available by market close on t for same-day features,

  • after-hours and non-trading-day news rolled to the next valid trading day,

  • no hidden future profile text,

  • no revised macro data used without vintage awareness.

Temporal alignment is not a small preprocessing detail. It is part of the scientific definition of the task.

6.8 Leakage

Leakage is any use of information unavailable at prediction time, including less obvious cases:

  • overlapping label windows,

  • future article inclusion,

  • scaler fit contamination,

  • adjusted-price errors,

  • profile text from the future,

  • revised external series treated as if point-in-time.

In this project, leakage is the most dangerous failure mode because financial signals are weak enough that small leakages can create convincing but false model improvements.

6.9 Benchmark comparability

Benchmark comparability is the property that two results can be fairly compared because they share:

  • the same universe definition,

  • same date coverage,

  • same splits,

  • same label logic,

  • same cutoff policy,

  • same feature-date rules,

  • same folds,

  • same metrics,

  • same filtering.

This should be treated as a formal research object, not an implicit assumption.

6.10 Modularity

Modularity matters here because it determines whether candidate ideas can be added and tested one at a time.

Good modularity means:

  • branch separability,

  • frozen upstream artifacts,

  • ablation cleanliness,

  • fair scenario-by-scenario comparison,

  • low risk of hidden benchmark drift.

6.11 Thesis contribution versus engineering expansion

A core danger of this project is confusing:
engineering breadth
with
thesis contribution.

A thesis contribution is not “we implemented many branches.”
A thesis contribution is closer to:
we showed, under disciplined evaluation, whether an event-state representation provides incremental predictive value, when it helps, and under what limits.

  1. Current architecture and pipeline proposal

8.1 Structural pipeline

The strongest current pipeline structure is:

raw data
-> canonical normalization
-> split-safe adjusted price branch
-> conservative market features
-> leakage-safe label construction
-> article normalization and alignment
-> offline embedding cache
-> daily event-state construction
-> final panel assembly keyed by ticker and date
-> temporal folds with purge and embargo
-> market-only baselines
-> first multimodal model
-> frozen prediction files
-> evaluation and ablation layer

That is a strong shape.

8.2 Raw data stage

Inputs:

  • daily OHLCV from Twelve Data,

  • ticker-scoped company news from Finnhub,

  • SEC submissions metadata for optional company KB,

  • explicit split-event source through provider-agnostic normalization.

Important note:
Current official vendor documentation confirms Twelve Data Basic still advertises 8 credits per minute and 800 per day, and their historical price guidance caps output at 5000 data points per request while recommending start_date and end_date for ranges. This supports the project’s incremental-update and pilot-first design. Twelve Data+2support.twelvedata.com+2

8.3 Processing and normalization stage

The processing logic should continue to enforce:

  • immutable raw payload preservation,

  • canonical interim schemas,

  • request ledgers and manifests,

  • timezone normalization,

  • deterministic deduplication,

  • raw and adjusted price separation,

  • explicit quality checks,

  • explicit split reports,

  • explicit as-of-close alignment annotations.

8.4 Event-state stage

The current event-state pipeline is conceptually right:

  • build article embeddings offline,

  • aggregate over a lookback window,

  • use recency weighting,

  • include scalar context such as news count and density,

  • enforce strict cutoff by official alignment rules,

  • avoid training-time text encoding for first-pass research.

That is good design for reproducibility and ablation control.

8.5 Labels stage

The current best-emerging label design is:

  • primary: forward excess return or abnormal return by horizon,

  • secondary: direction and downside labels,

  • optional later: uncertainty-aware targets.

This is stronger than raw return-only framing because it reduces the chance that the model is mostly learning market beta timing.

8.6 Model branch stage

Current best-emerging architecture:

  • market encoder,

  • event-state encoder,

  • simple fusion with gating,

  • per-horizon output heads.

That is exactly where the project should be right now.
It is not too simple.
It is not too flashy.
It is a good thesis-stage architecture because it is modular, explainable, and ablatable.

8.7 Evaluation stage

The evaluation stage should continue to operate only on:

  • frozen panels,

  • stored predictions,

  • frozen labels,

  • fixed folds,

  • fixed metrics,

  • declared comparability state.

That separation is one of the project’s strongest engineering-to-science decisions.

8.8 Retraining and update implications

The project should not yet overemphasize automated retraining or frequent update operations as part of the thesis contribution.

That would be premature.
The thesis is still about:

  • whether the event-state idea works,

  • under what evaluation discipline,

  • relative to which baselines,

  • for which horizons.

  1. Data processing and data control

9.1 Core processing logic

The project’s data processing logic should be governed by five principles:

  • raw is immutable,

  • canonical schemas are centralized,

  • adjusted prices are separate from raw prices,

  • feature generation happens only from canonical validated tables,

  • final panels are versioned and manifest-backed.

9.2 Split handling

Split handling remains one of the project’s most load-bearing correctness requirements.

If split handling fails:

  • labels are corrupted,

  • benchmark-relative features are distorted,

  • top-return outliers become mechanical artifacts,

  • model comparisons become invalid.

This is why the repository repeatedly places split handling before labels. That priority is correct.

9.3 Timestamp alignment

News alignment should remain strict:

  • only articles available by market close on t can enter features for t,

  • after-hours articles roll forward,

  • non-trading-day articles roll forward,

  • timezone normalization must happen before trade-date assignment.

The old research-design material included a stronger embargo-style delay for news. The current README and evaluation protocol instead define an as-of-close same-day policy. That is a meaningful conceptual change. It should be treated as a comparability boundary if older benchmark assumptions used an embargoed news window.

9.4 Duplicate news

News deduplication should remain explicit:

  • URL first,

  • text-hash fallback second,

  • source metadata preserved,

  • duplication statistics logged.

This is especially important if the project ever moves beyond Finnhub into mainstream source aggregation.

9.5 Provider limitations

Twelve Data:

  • Basic-tier quotas force incremental updates and pilot-first experiments.

  • Adjustment behavior must not be assumed from the vendor without verification.

  • Full-universe frequent refreshes are operationally fragile on Basic. Twelve Data+1

Finnhub:

  • company-news endpoint is a practical fit for ticker-scoped first-pass work, but historical completeness and throughput remain partly plan-dependent. Uncertain, verify manually. finnhub.io

SEC:

  • useful for identity and metadata, not automatically safe as a descriptive profile signal.

  • any time-varying descriptive use needs point-in-time discipline. sec.gov+1

9.6 Point-in-time discipline

Point-in-time discipline should be treated as a non-negotiable data-control theme.

This applies not only to news timestamps, but also to:

  • universe definition,

  • benchmark constituents,

  • market-relative labels,

  • firm descriptors,

  • macro data vintages,

  • revisions,

  • and any future KB branch.

9.7 Stale-risk and contract stability

Because the project now uses manifests and governance language around stale-risk and comparability, any change in:

  • label logic,

  • feature logic,

  • event-state pooling,

  • split-source strategy,

  • universe definition,

  • or fold logic
    should be treated as potentially benchmark-invalidating until explicitly reviewed.

That is good research hygiene.

  1. Blind spots, failure modes, and critical risks

10.1 Leakage channels

The project’s main leakage channels are:

  • after-hours news included too early,

  • non-trading-day news aligned incorrectly,

  • overlapping label windows not purged,

  • scaler fit contamination,

  • future descriptive profile information,

  • point-in-time violations in macro or firm context,

  • silent use of raw rather than adjusted prices,

  • factor-neutral targets computed with mismatched benchmark timing.

10.2 Corporate-action contamination

This remains a top-tier scientific risk.

The project already knows the stored Twelve Data history appears unadjusted at least for a tested AAPL split window. That means any label or feature family derived from raw OHLCV without explicit local back-adjustment is scientifically unsafe. The repository recognizes this, and the restart should preserve that severity. Twelve Data+1

10.3 Benchmark invalidation triggers

A benchmark should be treated as invalidated or at least not fully comparable if any of the following changes without controlled restaging:

  • target definitions,

  • split-source logic,

  • raw vs adjusted history usage,

  • news cutoff policy,

  • lookback logic,

  • universe definition,

  • final panel join filters,

  • fold generation,

  • metric definitions,

  • event-state aggregation rules.

10.4 Regime dependence

A model that works only in one market regime is not useless, but it is easy to overclaim.

The project’s horizons and modalities likely interact with regime:

  • event-state may help more in high-news or high-volatility periods,

  • medium horizons may be more stable than 1-day noise,

  • abnormal-return targets may be more robust than raw returns.

But strong regime claims need subgroup reporting, not intuition.

10.5 Survivorship issues

A current S&P 500 snapshot used historically can introduce survivorship bias.
The project already warns about this.
That warning should stay visible in the restart foundation.

10.6 Text timing errors

Text timing is more fragile than it looks.
Common errors include:

  • UTC normalization mistakes,

  • source timestamps interpreted in the wrong timezone,

  • missing after-hours handling,

  • articles without clear timestamp resolution,

  • source duplication creating false density.

10.7 Feature redundancy

This is directly relevant to your derivative proposal.

A major blind spot in feature engineering is confusing:
new transforms
with
new information.

Many transforms of OHLCV are heavily overlapping:

  • returns,

  • log returns,

  • momentum,

  • SMA gaps,

  • slopes,

  • second differences,

  • technical indicators,

  • trend proxies.

Without careful ablation, this becomes feature redundancy, not signal addition.

10.8 More-data-versus-more-signal confusion

This project is at real risk of mistaking:
more modalities,
more transforms,
more branches,
more architecture
for
more true predictive information.

The literature and the project’s own strongest documents both point to a harder truth:
largest gains may come from

  • better labels,

  • better split handling,

  • better temporal alignment,

  • better benchmark rigor,
    not from ever-richer architectures. papers.ssrn.com+2ScienceDirect+2

10.9 Modularity that harms comparability

Too much modularity can also hurt.
If every branch changes upstream filtering, label construction, or timing rules, then modularity becomes benchmark fragmentation.

The right modularity is:
branch-level separability on top of frozen common upstream artifacts.

10.10 Architecture complexity masking weak labels

A very strong warning:
if the target is weakly specified, noisy, or contaminated, richer architecture mostly improves the project’s ability to overfit or narrate itself.

This project should not use architecture to compensate for under-defended labels.

  1. Testing methodologies and validation philosophy

11.1 Conceptual testing stack

The project should rely on a layered testing philosophy:

  • unit logic tests,

  • data-contract tests,

  • pipeline and integrity tests,

  • temporal safety tests,

  • leakage tests,

  • benchmark comparability tests,

  • synthetic end-to-end mini-pipeline tests,

  • opt-in live provider tests,

  • human audit checks around critical windows such as known splits and known after-hours events.

11.2 What acceptable evidence should mean

A claim should be considered acceptable only if it has:

  • correct data-contract passage,

  • no known temporal leakage,

  • reproducible panel generation,

  • same row universe across compared models,

  • out-of-sample stored predictions,

  • fixed metrics and folds,

  • and a documented comparability state.

11.3 Walk-forward philosophy

Walk-forward is the correct conceptual center for this project because it reflects actual forecasting chronology and supports repeated regime exposure. Generic random splitting is not appropriate for this problem. papers.ssrn.com+1

11.4 Purge and embargo reasoning

Because the project uses forward-horizon labels, overlapping target windows can leak information even under chronological splitting. Purging and optional embargo are therefore not optional extras. They are part of the task definition for fair validation. papers.ssrn.com+1

11.5 Lockbox logic

A final untouched holdout or lockbox remains highly desirable for final thesis reporting, even if walk-forward drives model development. A single holdout is not sufficient for all model selection, but a final untouched block is valuable against repeated backtest selection. papers.ssrn.com

11.6 What should count as weak evidence

Weak evidence includes:

  • one recent holdout only,

  • one metric only,

  • no stored predictions,

  • no comparability record,

  • no split-window audit,

  • no subgroup stability view,

  • no discussion of missing horizons or alignment edge cases.

  1. Benchmarking philosophy and current benchmark interpretation

12.1 Benchmark philosophy

The benchmark philosophy should be:

predictive skill under strict temporal causality, with explicit overlap control, fixed artifacts, fair ablations, and horizon-specific interpretation.

That is much better than:
“best model wins.”

12.2 What should be benchmarked

At minimum:

  • market-only versus market-plus-event-state,

  • raw-label versus split-adjusted label sensitivity,

  • no-decay versus decay event-state pooling,

  • embeddings versus sentiment-only if that branch exists,

  • single-horizon versus multi-horizon training,

  • optional with-profile versus without-profile only after static metadata integration is stable.

12.3 What metrics matter

Primary benchmark family:

  • regression on forward excess or abnormal returns by horizon,

  • with Pearson and Spearman correlation,

  • plus cross-sectional ranking statistics such as daily IC and ICIR.

Secondary benchmark family:

  • direction and downside classification,

  • calibration and probabilistic scores only if uncertainty outputs are actually present.

This balance is better than relying on RMSE alone. A model can be weak in absolute numeric error but still provide useful cross-sectional ranking. That is especially true in noisy financial settings. ideas.repec.org+2sites.stat.washington.edu+2

12.4 When comparability is preserved versus broken

Preserved when:

  • same panel version,

  • same row universe,

  • same label definition,

  • same alignment policy,

  • same folds,

  • same metrics,

  • only one experimental factor changes.

Broken when:

  • different universes,

  • different missing-row filters,

  • different split logic,

  • different target definitions,

  • different horizon sets without clear handling,

  • different timing rules.

12.5 What benchmark claims should be treated cautiously

Treat cautiously:

  • any older hypothetical numeric improvements shown in RESEARCH_DESIGN_old.
    Those appear to be design examples, not repository-evidenced actual benchmark results.

  • any claim of provider completeness,

  • any claim of final thesis readiness from first-pass pilot outputs,

  • any architecture-comparison claim made before same-row-universe guarantees.

  1. Deep investigation of derivative-based feature ideas

13.1 Clarifying what derivative could mean here

In daily EOD market data, “derivative” is usually a discrete transform, not a true continuous derivative.

There are several distinct possibilities:

  • discrete first difference:
    close_t - close_t-1

  • percentage change:
    close_t / close_t-1 - 1

  • log return:
    log(close_t) - log(close_t-1)

  • rolling slope:
    slope of a linear fit over a window

  • second difference:
    x_t - 2x_t-1 + x_t-2

  • curvature-like transform:
    change in slope across a rolling window

  • derivative on smoothed series:
    first or second difference after smoothing

  • derivative on transformed OHLCV:
    for example on log close, normalized range, normalized volume, volatility, or cumulative returns rather than raw close

These are not equivalent.
And this is the first major critique of your proposal:
the phrase “compute derivatives on OHLCV” is too underspecified to be scientifically meaningful until normalized and disambiguated.

If by derivative you mean raw first differences on raw close:
that is usually inferior to returns or log returns.

If by second derivative you mean second differences on raw daily close:
that is usually a noise amplifier.

If by derivative over 5 to 30 days you mean rolling slope on log price or cumulative return:
that is much more defensible, but it is still mostly a trend or momentum proxy, not a fundamentally new family.

13.2 Evaluating derivative families across windows

13.2.1 Window = 1 day

Likely signal meaning:

  • immediate daily change,

  • shock reaction,

  • one-day acceleration if second-order.

What makes sense:

  • log return or simple return.
    What does not make much sense:

  • raw price difference across stocks with very different price levels.

Noise amplification risk:

  • very high for second difference,

  • moderate for first difference unless normalized.

Overlap with existing feature families:

  • almost total.
    A 1-day first derivative on close is basically return.
    A 1-day first derivative on volume is basically volume change.
    A 1-day second derivative is often just one-step acceleration noise.

Relation to event-state timing:

  • could matter for 1-day or 5-day targets if the project is modeling immediate absorption or reversal,

  • but if your news alignment is same-day as-of-close, then 1-day post-event interactions are already partly captured by returns and range features.

Interpretability:

  • high if phrased as return,

  • poor if phrased as raw derivative.

Leakage and comparability implications:

  • no special new leakage if computed past-only,

  • but can silently create comparability drift if you replace standard return features with raw differences.

Best use:

  • keep 1-day normalized return features.
    Do not sell them as novel derivatives.
    They are just baseline market features.

First-order versus second-order:

  • first-order yes, but in return or log-return form,

  • second-order low priority.

Verdict:
1-day derivative is only worth keeping if renamed to its standard financial interpretation.
As a “new idea,” it is weak.

13.2.2 Window = 5 days

Likely signal meaning:

  • short-run trend,

  • partial post-news drift,

  • very short medium-memory behavior.

What makes sense:

  • 5-day cumulative return,

  • rolling slope on log close,

  • change in volatility,

  • change in volume surprise.

Noise amplification risk:

  • moderate for first-order slope,

  • high for second-order curvature unless smoothed.

Overlap with existing feature families:

  • very high with momentum, trend, and SMA-gap style features.

Relation to event-state timing:

  • 5-day derivatives are more plausible than 1-day second derivatives because they may better align with partial information absorption.

Interpretability:

  • decent if defined as 5-day slope or 5-day cumulative return,

  • poor if defined as arbitrary finite-difference on raw OHLCV.

Leakage and comparability implications:

  • clean if computed past-only,

  • benchmark-clean if introduced as an additive ablation rather than replacing standard momentum features.

Best use:

  • optional trend proxy.

First-order versus second-order:

  • first-order plausible,

  • second-order only plausible if computed on a smoothed transformed series.

Verdict:
reasonable as an optional ablation, not as a core thesis innovation.

13.2.3 Window = 10 days

Likely signal meaning:

  • short-to-intermediate trend,

  • persistence or reversal in information absorption.

Strength:

  • may be somewhat more stable than 5-day.

Weakness:

  • even more overlap with momentum and trend features already recommended by the repo.

Noise amplification risk:

  • manageable for first-order slope,

  • still high for second-order on unsmoothed data.

Relation to event-state timing:

  • might align better with 5-day and 20-day targets than 1-day derivatives do.

Verdict:
usable as a trend proxy, but still not a distinct core family.

13.2.4 Window = 15 days

Likely signal meaning:

  • intermediate trend.

Problem:

  • this window is not standard enough to offer clear conceptual advantage over 10 or 20.
    It risks becoming a convenience number rather than a motivated one.

Overlap:

  • extremely high with momentum families and cumulative-return features.

Verdict:
low priority. Likely feature bloat unless strong ablation evidence emerges.

13.2.5 Window = 20 days

Likely signal meaning:

  • approximately monthly trend,

  • medium-horizon persistence,

  • slower repricing context.

This is the first window where the concept becomes more naturally aligned with a 20-day horizon target.

Still, the core critique remains:
a 20-day first derivative or slope on transformed price is mostly a momentum/trend feature by another name.

That is not useless.
It is just not novel.

Second-order 20-day curvature could theoretically capture acceleration versus deceleration of trend, but in daily equities this is fragile and highly dependent on smoothing choice.

Verdict:
20-day slope-type features are plausible and maybe useful.
But they belong in the momentum/trend family, not a new derivative family.

13.2.6 Window = 30 days

Likely signal meaning:

  • slow trend,

  • narrative persistence,

  • broader medium-run context.

Potential relevance:

  • might help 20-day and 60-day horizons more than shorter horizons.

Major critique:

  • 30-day derivatives are very likely to be redundant with:

    • 20-day momentum,

    • moving-average gaps,

    • rolling beta/context,

    • regime features.

Second-order 30-day derivatives are especially suspect.
At that point you are extracting curvature from already smoothed monthly behavior. That can become numer

That statement is already aligned with the repo and with the more defensible branch of the literature.   1. FIFTH, DEFINE THE DERIVATIVE IDEA PRECISELY BEFORE TESTING IT

Right now, “compute derivatives of OHLCV” is too vague.

You need to distinguish at least six different families:

  • raw first differences
    open_t - open_t-1, close_t - close_t-1, and so on

  • percentage changes
    (x_t / x_t-k) - 1

  • log differences
    log(x_t) - log(x_t-k)

  • rolling slope estimates
    regression slope over the last k days

  • second differences
    x_t - 2x_t-1 + x_t-2 or analogous multi-step discrete curvature

  • derivatives on transformed rather than raw series
    for example on log close, range, rolling volatility, volume surprise, or benchmark-relative residuals

This distinction matters because these are not equivalent scientifically.

Hard criticism:
If you say “derivative” but actually mean simple returns or rolling slopes, then the idea is not new. It is mostly a relabeling of standard time-series features. If you truly mean second-order discrete curvature on daily OHLCV, then the idea is new only in the weak sense that many low-value noisy transforms can be invented. Novelty is not value.

  1. SIXTH, HARD CRITIQUE OF FIRST- AND SECOND-DERIVATIVE FEATURES

STRONGEST ARGUMENT IN FAVOR

The best argument for derivative-style features is that event-state models should react not just to the level of market variables, but to changing market motion. In plain words, the news branch may interact more naturally with acceleration, reversal, and trend-change proxies than with absolute price or raw volume levels. A good event-state system should care about whether the market was already moving, decelerating, or snapping back when the news arrived.

That is the best pro-derivative argument.

STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST

Most of what you probably want from “derivatives” is already captured more cleanly by simpler and more standard features:

  • returns

  • log returns

  • rolling momentum

  • rolling volatility

  • intraday range

  • volume surprise

  • benchmark-relative returns

  • reversal features

  • slope on smoothed series

In other words, the derivative idea is in real danger of being false sophistication.

For daily OHLCV, naive first differences on open, high, low, and close are usually scale-dependent and less defensible than return-style normalization. Naive second differences are even more dangerous because they amplify noise, outliers, and corporate-action imperfections. If split handling is imperfect, second-order transforms can become garbage extremely fast.

This is especially true in your setting because the project is not pure technical forecasting. It is event-state forecasting. The market branch is supposed to complement the text branch, not become an uncontrolled feature explosion machine.

WINDOW-BY-WINDOW CRITIQUE

1-DAY

  • first-order derivative meaning:
    essentially immediate change or local motion

  • value:
    some value, but only if expressed as return-like or normalized change

  • critique:
    raw first differences are inferior to returns or log returns

  • second-order critique:
    at 1-day daily resolution, second differences are often mostly noise unless strongly smoothed first

Verdict:
1-day derivative ideas are only worth keeping if translated into normalized return or reversal-style features. Raw discrete derivatives on raw OHLC are weak.

5-DAY

  • meaning:
    short trend or short reaction absorption

  • value:
    better than 1-day for event-state interaction because it may catch drift or partial post-news adjustment

  • critique:
    still substantially overlaps with 5-day momentum and rolling slope

  • second-order critique:
    can sometimes act as reversal proxy, but volatility-regime dependence is strong

Verdict:
Reasonable as an experiment, but should compete directly against simple 5-day return, 5-day slope, and reversal features. It is not automatically better.

10-DAY

  • meaning:
    medium-short trend persistence

  • value:
    potentially better aligned with event-state persistence than 1-day noise

  • critique:
    heavy overlap with standard momentum windows and event-state lookback choices

Verdict:
Testable, but not core. Mostly redundant unless combined with regime conditioning.

15-DAY

  • meaning:
    midpoint between short drift and medium repricing

  • critique:
    awkward window. It is neither standard nor strongly interpretable. It increases search space more than insight.

Verdict:
Low priority. Very easy to overfit by window shopping.

20-DAY

  • meaning:
    medium-horizon repricing proxy, close to one trading month

  • value:
    this is the first derivative-style window that actually has a clear thesis interpretation in your setting

  • critique:
    should still be compared to 20-day momentum, rolling slope, and residual-return trends

Verdict:
Worth testing narrowly, but only as part of a disciplined small ablation set.

30-DAY

  • meaning:
    slower narrative absorption or medium-term drift

  • value:
    can matter if your event state has longer persistence and if horizons include 20 or 60 trading days

  • critique:
    very likely to blur multiple regimes and overlapping events; also less useful if your target is only 1, 5, 20 days

Possible extension. Not core for the first restart wave.

OVERALL VERDICT ON FIRST-ORDER DERIVATIVES

Classification:

  • not core

  • optional experiment

  • maybe a strong extension only if implemented as normalized, interpretable transforms

OVERALL VERDICT ON SECOND-ORDER DERIVATIVES

Classification:

  • attractive but risky

  • probably not worth prioritizing early

  • easy to make noisy, unstable, and benchmark-dirty

My hard criticism:
Second-order derivatives on daily OHLCV are exactly the kind of feature family that looks mathematically appealing, feels “deeper,” and often contributes much less than expected. In many financial ML projects, this kind of idea survives because it sounds intellectually rich, not because it survives serious ablation.

  1. WHAT TO TEST INSTEAD OF OR BEFORE DERIVATIVES

These feature families are more defensible than raw derivative families.

A. SIMPLE AND LOG RETURNS
These should remain the baseline motion features because they are normalized, interpretable, and standard.

B. ROLLING MOMENTUM
Use 5, 10, 20-day normalized return-style momentum before inventing derivative jargon. This is usually the cleaner version of what you are trying to capture.

C. ROLLING VOLATILITY
Important because news effects often differ by volatility regime.

D. RANGE-BASED FEATURES
Intraday range, close-to-high, close-to-low, and range compression/expansion are often more meaningful than second derivatives of close.

E. VOLUME-PRICE INTERACTION
Examples:

  • signed volume surprise

  • abnormal volume with return sign

  • volume spike with weak price follow-through
    These can be much more event-relevant than curvature on OHLC.

F. BENCHMARK-RELATIVE OR RESIDUAL FEATURES
If the market is already moving strongly, raw stock moves are confounded. Residualization or benchmark-relative features may be more valuable than derivatives.

G. REGIME FEATURES
Simple regime indicators such as recent realized volatility, market drawdown state, or benchmark trend state may dominate many derivative-style experiments because they directly address heterogeneity in news response.

  1. THE BENCHMARK-SAFE EXPERIMENT LADDER

You asked for detailed instructions. This is the clean experiment order.

STEP 1
Freeze one primary dataset version.
Do not keep changing upstream cleaning while testing downstream models.

STEP 2
Freeze one primary target family.
Recommended:

  • excess returns at 1, 5, 20 days

STEP 3
Freeze one market-only baseline family.
Recommended:

  • ridge

  • elastic net

  • simple market MLP

STEP 4
Freeze one event-state baseline.
Recommended:

  • offline embeddings

  • one lookback

  • one decay rule

  • no attention

  • no end-to-end text fine-tuning

STEP 5
Run market-only versus market-plus-event-state.
That is the real thesis baseline comparison.

STEP 6
Only after that, run small, disciplined feature-family ablations:

  • no derivative family

  • normalized first-order family only

  • slope family

  • derivative plus regime features

  • derivative plus volume interaction
    No more than a few variants in the first wave.

STEP 7
If derivative features help, test whether they still help after simpler competitors are added:

  • returns

  • momentum

  • volatility

  • range

  • volume surprise
    If the derivative gain disappears, it was probably redundant.

STEP 8
Only after the above is stable, consider stronger extensions:

  • static company profile branch

  • uncertainty-aware outputs

  • relation-aware methods

  • more advanced fusion

This order matches the repo’s already encoded philosophy: correctness before sophistication, split handling before labels, baselines before multimodal expansion, frozen artifacts before training.

  1. WHAT SHOULD COUNT AS ACCEPTABLE EVIDENCE

A result should not count as a thesis-strength result unless all of the following are true:

  • temporal split is strictly chronological

  • purge and embargo are applied correctly for the chosen horizons

  • article cutoff obeys as-of-close policy

  • labels come from adjusted prices

  • stored predictions are evaluated against frozen labels

  • the comparison changes only one major factor at a time

Your evaluation protocol already encodes most of this. That is good. Preserve it. Do not loosen it just to make experiments easier.

This is also consistent with the broader finance-ML literature: purged or embargo-aware validation is motivated precisely because overlapping label windows and temporal dependence can leak information into training, while repeated strategy search creates backtest overfitting risk. philpapers.org+3papers.ssrn.com+3papers.ssrn.com+3

  1. WHAT THE BROADER LITERATURE SUPPORTS MOST STRONGLY

EVENT-DRIVEN FAMILY
Ding et al. remain the classic reference for event-driven stock prediction. Their work supports the broad family, not your exact implementation choice. It supports the legitimacy of combining structured event or text-derived information with market prediction, but it does not automatically justify your exact event-state formulation. ijcai.org

FINANCIAL TEXT REPRESENTATION
FinBERT supports the idea that finance-specific language models can outperform generic machine learning methods on financial sentiment tasks. That supports using domain-specific text representations later, but it does not mean you should jump to full fine-tuning now. A frozen embedding pipeline is still the cleaner first thesis move. arXiv+1

MULTI-HORIZON ARCHITECTURES
Temporal Fusion Transformer is relevant because it formalizes multi-horizon forecasting with mixed covariate types and gating. It supports the idea that horizon-specific outputs and controlled feature selection are legitimate architectural directions. It does not prove TFT is the right model for your project. It proves the family is legitimate. arXiv

PROBABILISTIC OUTPUTS
Gneiting and Raftery are foundational for proper scoring rules. This matters if you later add uncertainty heads, quantiles, or probabilistic downside outputs. Proper scoring rules are the correct framework for evaluating probabilistic forecasts honestly. sites.stat.washington.edu

FORECAST COMPARISON
Diebold-Mariano and Giacomini-White matter because once you have stored predictions from competing models, simple point comparisons are not enough. Forecast-comparison tests and conditional predictive ability tests become relevant for stronger claims. NBER+1

MULTIMODAL FINANCE
Recent multimodal finance papers show that heterogeneous sources can help, but they also confirm a danger you should take seriously: more modalities do not automatically mean better science. Fusion design, modality weighting, window choice, and dataset scope all strongly affect outcomes. The more modern multimodal papers are useful as idea maps, but they do not remove the need for disciplined ablations and benchmark fairness. ScienceDirect+1

  1. REPO-AWARE IMMEDIATE NEXT STEPS

The repo already has first-pass support across ingestion, adjustment, features, event states, modeling panels, baselines, multimodal training, and evaluation. The remaining priorities in the repo documents are documentation hardening, reporting polish, selected multimodal extensions, and manual verification of live provider behavior. Also, the practical runbook notes that while the repo has dedicated CLIs for universe freezing, split-event creation, and adjusted prices, it still lacks dedicated CLIs for embedding-cache and event-state batch generation.

That means your immediate next research tasks should be:

  • stabilize one canonical dataset version

  • stabilize one canonical market-only benchmark

  • stabilize one canonical event-state benchmark

  • define the first derivative ablation set narrowly

  • verify live provider realities before treating any pilot result as final

  1. WHAT TO CLASSIFY AS CORE, EXTENSION, OPTIONAL, OR REJECT

CORE NOW

  • adjusted-price based labels

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • market-only baselines

  • first multimodal event-state model

  • walk-forward plus purge and embargo

STRONG NEXT-STEP CANDIDATES

  • static company metadata branch

  • richer reporting and statistical comparison

EXTENSION IF TIME ALLOWS

  • normalized first-order derivative family

  • rolling slope features

  • selected volume-price interaction experiments

ATTRACTIVE BUT RISKY

PROBABLY NOT WORTH PRIORITIZING NOW

  • early end-to-end text fine-tuning

  • adding many auxiliary modalities before benchmark discipline is mature

  1. THE MOST IMPORTANT WARNING

Do not confuse “more mathematically transformed features” with “more signal.”

In this project, the biggest real risks are not lack of feature cleverness. They are:

  • weak target discipline

  • hidden leakage

  • broken comparability

  • window shopping

  • excessive ablation breadth

  • architecture complexity masking label weakness

  • provider reality mismatches

Those are the mistakes most likely to damage the thesis.

  1. SELECTED SUPPORTING REFERENCES FOR THIS CONTINUATION

[P1]
Deep Learning for Event-Driven Stock Prediction
Xiao Ding, Yue Zhang, Ting Liu, Junwen Duan
2015, IJCAI
Why it matters:
Classical event-driven stock prediction reference; supports the legitimacy of event-informed forecasting but is more event-extraction-centered than your evolving event-state framing.
Link:
https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/15/Papers/329.pdf ijcai.org

[P2]
FinBERT: Financial Sentiment Analysis with Pre-trained Language Models
Dogu Araci
2019, arXiv
Why it matters:
Supports finance-domain language representations; useful for later text-branch strengthening, but not proof that end-to-end text fine-tuning should be early priority.
Link:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10063 arXiv+1

[P3]
Temporal Fusion Transformers for Interpretable Multi-horizon Time Series Forecasting
Bryan Lim, Sercan Arik, Nicolas Loeff, Tomas Pfister
2019 preprint, 2021 International Journal of Forecasting
Why it matters:
Strong multi-horizon architecture reference; supports shared representation plus horizon-specific outputs and gating logic.

Tilmann Gneiting, Adrian E. Raftery
2007, Journal of the American Statistical Association

FINAL CONTINUATION CONCLUSION

The project should now treat its core as:

  • event-state plus market-context forecasting

  • under strict EOD alignment

  • with excess-return style targets

  • benchmarked against disciplined market-only baselines

The derivative proposal is not worthless, but it is not strong enough to become a core pillar right now.

My direct classification is:

  • first-order normalized derivative-like features:
    optional experiment, maybe strong extension if kept narrow

  • second-order daily OHLCV derivatives across many windows:
    attractive but likely low-ROI and noisy; do not prioritize early

The strongest unresolved questions are now:

  • how much incremental value event state adds beyond market-only

  • which horizon benefits most

  • whether normalized motion features add more than simpler momentum/range/volume families

  • whether any gain survives strict benchmark discipline

What should definitely not happen next:

  • no giant feature explosion

  • no premature graph or MoE branch

  • no broad derivative window shopping

  • no target redesign and architecture redesign at the same time

  • no thesis claims from pilot results before manual provider verification

What should be stabilized before any major new implementation wave:

  • one canonical dataset version

  • one canonical target family

  • one canonical market-only baseline

  • one canonical event-state baseline

  • one narrow ablation ladder

That is the clean continuation point.

<< 22. CONCRETE EXPERIMENT MATRIX, EXACT ABLATIONS, AND STOP/GO CRITERIA >>

This continuation turns the restart into a controlled research program instead of a vague exploration.

The repo is already strong enough for pilot experiments, debugging, methodological validation, market-only training, first multimodal training, and evaluation/ablation summaries. The remaining priorities are documentation hardening, reporting polish, selected multimodal extensions, and manual external verification. That means the next phase should not be “invent more architecture.” It should be “run the cleanest possible evidence ladder.”

The practical runbook already recommends:

  • pilot10 first

  • hashing backend first for cheap end-to-end validation

  • ridge baseline first

  • first multimodal model second

  • then scaled experiment subsets such as 30 to 100 stocks, not 503 immediately

  • and explicit caution around Twelve Data quota pressure and Finnhub historical completeness uncertainty.

So the correct next move is not to improvise. It is to use a staged experiment matrix with frozen rules.

<< 22.1 GLOBAL RESEARCH FREEZE RULES >>

Before the first serious experiment wave, freeze these items:

  • one primary target family

    • forward excess returns at 1, 5, and 20 trading days

  • one canonical market benchmark

    • one benchmark series only for the whole wave

  • one canonical universe file per wave

    • pilot10 for pilot

    • one experiment50 or experiment100 file for thesis-core runs

  • one canonical split-adjustment policy

  • one canonical article text variant

    • headline only or headline plus summary, but not both inside the same wave

  • one canonical event-state default

    • one lookback

    • one decay policy

    • one embedding backend

  • one canonical temporal validation policy

    • same walk-forward, purge, and embargo configuration for all comparable runs

If you change any of the above, you are not running “another model.” You are starting a new benchmark family.

That matters because the repo’s architecture and evaluation protocol are explicitly built around frozen datasets, saved predictions, purge-aware chronology, and as-of-close alignment. Comparability is one of the core scientific assets of the project.

<< 22.2 HARD GATE BEFORE ANY MODELING >>

Do not allow any model training to count if any of these fail:

  • split-adjustment audit fails

    • known split windows still show mechanical false jumps

  • article cutoff audit fails

    • after-hours or non-trading-day mapping is wrong

  • final panel uniqueness fails

    • more than one row per ticker/date

  • train/validation/test chronology fails

  • scaler-fit contamination fails

  • Finnhub historical coverage is too sparse for the chosen date range to make the text branch meaningful

  • benchmark series is missing or inconsistently aligned

The evaluation protocol already makes chronology, overlap handling, and saved-prediction evaluation first-class constraints, and the architecture overview explicitly states that split logic must remain explicit and alignment logic must remain centralized. Preserve that discipline.

My direct criticism:
A surprising number of finance ML projects treat these as engineering details. They are not. They are the difference between a thesis and a toy.

<< 22.3 THE EXPERIMENT LADDER >>

Use the following experiment IDs and do not skip upward.

<< E00 — DATA AND INTEGRITY GATE >>
Purpose

  • verify that the dataset itself is not invalidating the thesis before any model discussion

What is fixed

  • chosen universe file

  • chosen time span

  • chosen benchmark

  • chosen split source

  • chosen news source and text variant

What is checked

  • price continuity

  • split diagnostics

  • duplicate article rate

  • no-news rate by ticker

  • final panel coverage

  • label availability by horizon

Stop/go rule

  • GO only if the adjusted-price branch is auditable, article alignment is stable, and the final modeling panel has enough rows across all three horizons to make walk-forward evaluation meaningful

  • STOP if the text branch is too sparse in the chosen window

  • STOP if split windows still contaminate labels

This is not optional. It is the precondition for the whole thesis.

<< E01 — TRIVIAL BASELINES >>
Purpose

  • confirm that the task is not being measured against an absurdly weak baseline

Models

  • constant predictor

  • simple OLS

  • ridge

Metrics

  • MAE

  • RMSE

  • R^2

  • Pearson

  • Spearman

  • direction accuracy only as secondary

Go rule

  • GO if ridge beats trivial baseline on at least one main horizon in out-of-sample evaluation

  • STOP if nothing beats trivial by a meaningful margin, because then either the target, features, or evaluation setup needs inspection before neural models are justified

Hard criticism

  • If you skip this, later neural improvements become scientifically weak because you never established that the problem was learnable under conservative baselines.

<< E02 — MARKET-ONLY THESIS BASELINE >>
Purpose

  • establish the clean non-text baseline that all multimodal claims must beat

Models

  • ridge

  • elastic net

  • market-only MLP

Fixed inputs

  • conservative market features only

  • no text branch

  • no company branch

Primary decision rule

  • choose one market-only baseline family for the rest of the wave

  • usually the strongest of ridge or market MLP, but do not keep switching winner by horizon unless you explicitly define a per-horizon benchmark policy

Proposed stop/go rule

  • GO if at least one market-only model achieves usable out-of-sample signal on at least one horizon

  • use the earlier research design threshold of R^2 > 0.05 on at least one horizon as an aspirational marker, not a rigid truth law

  • if all market-only baselines are very weak, pause and inspect target design, universe choice, and benchmark-relative formulation before adding text

Hard criticism

  • If the market-only branch is weak everywhere, a later multimodal gain may simply be exploiting implementation asymmetries or data sparsity quirks.

<< E03 — CORE THESIS TEST: MARKET-ONLY VS EVENT-STATE MULTIMODAL >>
Purpose

  • the real main hypothesis test

Models

  • chosen market-only winner from E02

  • first-pass multimodal model with market branch plus event-state branch

Fixed inputs

  • same universe

  • same date range

  • same targets

  • same folds

  • same metric set

  • same benchmark

  • same train/validation/test policy

Main question

  • does event state add incremental value beyond market-only?

Primary decision rule

  • evaluate delta against the market-only winner, not against OLS

  • report fold means, spread, and paired prediction comparison

Proposed stop/go rule

  • strong GO: positive delta on 5d and 20d with consistent sign across most folds

  • moderate GO: positive overall delta but concentrated in high-news-density windows

  • STOP for “core-thesis strength” if improvements are inconsistent, only appear on one lucky period, or disappear under paired comparison

The earlier research design suggested a target of delta R^2 >= 0.02 on 5d and 20d as a directional hypothesis. That is acceptable as a stretch target, but too aggressive to be treated as the only definition of success. Keep it as a strong-success marker, not a binary law.

Hard criticism

  • If the multimodal gain is tiny, unstable, and expensive, the thesis should not pretend it discovered a strong event-state effect.

  • A small but robust gain is better than a flashy but fragile one.

<< E04 — DECAY POLICY ABLATION >>
Purpose

  • test whether the event-state branch needs temporal weighting or not

Variants

  • simple mean

  • exponential decay

  • linear decay

Hold constant

  • same embeddings

  • same lookback

  • same architecture

  • same folds

  • same targets

Decision rule

  • if exponential wins consistently, keep it as default

  • if gains are tiny and inconsistent, prefer the simpler mean for thesis cleanliness

  • if decay only helps on long horizons, state that explicitly instead of pretending it is universally better

The old research design already treats this as one of the core ablations.

Hard criticism

  • Do not force a decay story if the difference is negligible. A cleaner thesis with mean pooling can be stronger than a decorative half-life parameter with weak evidence.

<< E05 — EMBEDDING FAMILY ABLATION >>
Purpose

  • test whether semantic representation really matters, or whether coarse sentiment-like signals are enough

Variants

  • hashing backend only for smoke testing, not for final claims

  • sentence-transformer dense embeddings

  • sentiment-only proxy baseline if you implement one

  • dense embeddings plus novelty scalar if available

Stop/go rule

  • GO for dense embeddings as thesis default only if they beat sentiment-only style variants and justify their computation cost

  • STOP early on expensive embedding escalation if simple dense embeddings already saturate the benefit

Hard criticism

  • Do not confuse “more expensive NLP” with “better thesis.”

  • Frozen dense embeddings are likely the sweet spot early.

  • End-to-end text fine-tuning should stay blocked unless the simpler text branch already proved meaningful.

<< E06 — LOOKBACK WINDOW ABLATION >>
Purpose

  • test event-state memory length

Variants

  • 7 days

  • 14 days

  • 30 days

Interpretation rule

  • if short windows help only 1d and 5d, while longer windows help 20d, that is a coherent result

  • if 30d wins everywhere only marginally, consider whether it is just acting as a noise-averaging prior rather than truly capturing event persistence

  • if 30d harms 1d but helps 20d, preserve the asymmetry instead of collapsing to one narrative

The old research design already proposed longer history helping longer horizons only. That is a reasonable working hypothesis.

Hard criticism

  • Do not expand this into many arbitrary windows like 9, 12, 17, 23, 45. That becomes window shopping.

<< E07 — MULTI-HORIZON VS SINGLE-HORIZON >>
Purpose

  • test whether shared representation across horizons is helping or diluting

Variants

  • one multi-task model

  • one separate model per horizon

Decision rule

  • if multi-task is slightly worse but much simpler and more stable, it may still be preferred for thesis coherence

  • if single-horizon is materially better, preserve that result honestly even if it complicates the narrative

Hard criticism

  • Multi-horizon elegance is not automatically better science.

  • If shared learning hurts the key horizon, you should not keep it just because it looks more sophisticated.

<< E08 — DERIVATIVE FEATURE FAMILY ABLATION >>
Purpose

  • test your proposal without letting it hijack the project

Important constraint

  • this experiment must come after E02 through E07

  • not before

Tested variants

  • baseline market features only

  • baseline plus normalized first-order motion family

  • baseline plus rolling slope family

  • baseline plus second-order family

  • baseline plus derivative family plus regime features

Mandatory comparison set

  • returns

  • log returns

  • momentum

  • rolling volatility

  • range features

  • volume surprise

  • derivative family

Exact rule

  • do not test derivatives in isolation against nothing

  • test whether they add value after stronger standard alternatives are already present

Stop/go rule

  • GO only if derivative-style features improve out-of-sample results beyond the stronger simpler alternatives, not just beyond a weak baseline

  • STOP if gains vanish once momentum, volatility, range, and volume interactions are present

  • STOP if second-order derivatives help only in one fold or one narrow window

Hard criticism

  • This is where most elegant but low-value ideas die, and that is good.

  • If derivatives lose here, they should be demoted to appendix-level or rejected.

<< E09 — NEWS-DENSITY HETEROGENEITY >>
Purpose

  • test whether text helps mostly when there is enough text to matter

Subgroups

  • stock-days split into news-density quintiles

Decision rule

  • if multimodal gains are concentrated in Q4 and Q5, that is still a valid and interesting thesis result

  • if the text branch only helps when there is actual information flow, that supports the event-state framing

This was already part of the earlier research design hypotheses and should be preserved.

Hard criticism

  • If the text branch fails overall but clearly helps in event-dense slices, do not throw it away too early. The correct conclusion may be conditional usefulness, not universal uselessness.

<< E10 — TIME-PERIOD STABILITY >>
Purpose

  • test whether the result is regime-fragile

Slices

  • by year

  • by broad market regime if you later define one

Decision rule

  • GO if gains are not purely concentrated in one exceptional period

  • if one year dominates the benefit, the thesis must report fragility honestly

This also exists in the earlier design and is scientifically important.

<< E11 — OPTIONAL STATIC COMPANY METADATA BRANCH >>
Purpose

  • test whether cheap static firm context improves the model without leakage explosion

Variants

  • market only

  • market plus event state

  • market plus event state plus static company metadata

Decision rule

  • only run after core event-state value is established

  • if static metadata gives a small but robust gain, it is a good thesis extension

  • if it complicates the panel and gives negligible value, leave it out of the core thesis

Hard criticism

  • This is extension territory, not the first proof-of-value experiment.

<< 22.4 PROPOSED EXACT RESEARCH WAVES >>

<< WAVE 1 — INTEGRITY AND BENCHMARK FOUNDATION >>
Experiments

  • E00

  • E01

  • E02

  • E03

Goal

  • prove that the dataset is valid

  • prove that market-only learning is nontrivial

  • test the main event-state hypothesis once

Hard stop conditions

  • split contamination unresolved

  • Finnhub coverage too weak

  • multimodal improvement absent and market-only also weak

  • fold instability too large to interpret

Output of Wave 1

  • one frozen baseline result table

  • one frozen market-only vs multimodal comparison

  • one go/no-go decision on whether the thesis core is empirically alive

<< WAVE 2 — EVENT-STATE SHAPE >>
Experiments

  • E04

  • E05

  • E06

  • E07

  • E09

  • E10

Goal

  • determine what kind of text memory and representation is actually useful

  • determine whether usefulness is conditional on density or regime

  • determine whether multi-horizon coupling helps or hurts

Hard stop conditions

  • every event-state variation is fragile or inconsistent

  • text improvements vanish under subgroup or year slicing

  • one configuration looks best only because of one lucky fold

Output of Wave 2

  • one canonical event-state design

  • one honest statement of where text helps and where it does not

<< WAVE 3 — DERIVATIVE AND COMPETING FEATURE FAMILIES >>
Experiments

  • E08

Goal

  • test your derivative idea under fair, benchmark-clean conditions

Hard stop conditions

  • gains disappear against simpler alternatives

  • second-order transforms are unstable

  • complexity grows faster than explanatory value

Output of Wave 3

  • keep as strong extension

  • keep as optional appendix experiment

  • or reject

<< WAVE 4 — EXTENSIONS >>
Experiments

  • E11

  • later uncertainty-aware or richer multimodal branches only if justified

Goal

  • add thesis extensions without corrupting the core benchmark ladder

<< 22.5 EXACT STOP/GO POLICY FOR THE DERIVATIVE IDEA >>

Because you asked for hard criticism, here is the cleanest policy.

GREEN LIGHT

  • normalized first-order derivative-like transforms beat a strong simpler market-feature set

  • gains are present in more than one fold

  • gains survive 5d and 20d horizons better than 1d-only luck

  • interpretation remains clean

YELLOW LIGHT

  • small improvement only when paired with regime features

  • improvement only on one horizon

  • improvement only in event-dense or high-volatility subsets

  • useful as extension, not core

RED LIGHT

  • only raw first differences help, not normalized variants

  • second-order family looks best only before proper alternative comparisons

  • gains vanish after adding momentum, volatility, range, and volume surprise

  • fold variability is high

  • explanation becomes “it seems mathematically richer” rather than “it adds reproducible signal”

My recommendation remains:

  • first-order normalized variants are worth a narrow, disciplined test later

  • second-order family should be treated as high-risk appendix territory unless it proves unexpectedly robust

<< 22.6 EXACT REPORTING RULES FOR EACH EXPERIMENT >>

For every experiment, report all of the following:

  • fixed components

  • changed component

  • universe file

  • time span

  • split source

  • benchmark series

  • target family

  • fold policy

  • metrics used

  • mean across folds

  • spread across folds

  • paired comparison against the immediately relevant baseline

  • runtime burden

  • interpretation

  • benchmark comparability status

If any experiment changes target design, universe, split policy, benchmark series, or time period substantially, it must be reported as a new benchmark family, not as a simple ablation.

<< 22.7 WHAT YOU SHOULD NOT TEST YET >>

Do not test these in the first serious thesis wave:

  • time-varying company profile branches

  • full raw mainstream news integration

  • graph or relation-aware models

  • mixture-of-experts routing

  • end-to-end text fine-tuning

  • probabilistic heads as core outputs

  • a huge indicator zoo

  • massive derivative window grids

  • all-503 live experiments

The repo documents are already warning in the same direction: richer multimodal architectures, company-profile training support, uncertainty-aware outputs, and stronger ablation coverage are remaining priorities after the first-pass foundation, not before it. Manual external verification is also still pending.

<< 22.8 THE SHORTEST HONEST THESIS PATH >>

If you had to keep the thesis narrow and strong, the cleanest path is:

  • adjusted prices

  • strict EOD aligned company news

  • conservative market features

  • frozen dense embeddings

  • exponential-decay or mean event state

  • market-only vs multimodal comparison

  • multi-horizon excess-return evaluation

  • density and regime subgroup analysis

  • one narrow derivative-family appendix experiment at the end

That path preserves:

  • scientific cleanliness

  • benchmark comparability

  • manageable scope

  • defendable narrative

  • and a strong chance of actually finishing

<< 22.9 FINAL DECISION RULE FOR THE NEXT STEP >>

Your next actual research move should be:

  • run Wave 1 fully

  • do not touch derivative experiments before Wave 1 and Wave 2

  • treat the derivative idea as a controlled late-stage challenger, not as a founding pillar

  • treat any unstable but interesting result as extension-level, not core-thesis truth

The repo is already architecturally aligned with that approach because it has first-pass support for ingestion, split handling, labels, embeddings, event-state aggregation, walk-forward validation, baseline training, multimodal training, and evaluation/ablation tooling, while still explicitly identifying reporting polish, documentation hardening, and carefully selected extensions as the remaining priorities.
