<< 23. EXACT HYPOTHESES, NUMERIC ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLDS, FAILURE INTERPRETATIONS, AND THESIS-READY RESULT TABLE TEMPLATES >>

This section converts the restart into a decision system.

The project is already in late foundation / early experimentation, with first-pass support for:

  • adjusted prices

  • event-state aggregation

  • final modeling panels

  • market-only baselines

  • first multimodal training

  • stored-prediction evaluation

  • ablation tooling

That means the next research phase should not ask, “What else can we add?”
It should ask, “What exact evidence would count as success, partial success, failure, or extension-only value?”

<< 23.1 HOW TO USE THRESHOLDS CORRECTLY >>

The numeric thresholds below should be treated as:

  • strong success markers

  • not divine laws

  • not excuses for p-hacking

  • not reasons to hide informative negative results

In finance ML, a result can be scientifically useful even when it misses an aggressive threshold, if it is:

  • stable

  • reproducible

  • correctly benchmarked

  • theoretically coherent

  • and honestly delimited

At the same time, weak and unstable gains should not be dressed up as success. The repo’s evaluation rules already prioritize out-of-sample time integrity, purge and embargo logic, frozen predictions, and same-rule comparison. Those constraints matter more than cosmetic metric improvements.

So use the thresholds in three bands:

  • Strong support

  • Weak or conditional support

  • Failure or non-support

That three-band structure is much better than pretending everything is binary.

<< 23.2 CORE THESIS HYPOTHESIS GRID >>

Use the following project-level hypothesis set as the official restart basis.

H1a — MARKET-ONLY LEARNABILITY

Statement
A properly regularized market-only model should achieve non-trivial out-of-sample predictive value on at least one horizon.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • R^2 > 0.05 on at least one horizon

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    R^2 > 0.05 on at least one main horizon

  • Weak support:
    R^2 between 0.02 and 0.05 with consistent sign across folds and reasonable ranking correlation

  • Failure:
    R^2 near zero or negative everywhere, with no stable ranking usefulness

What failure would mean

  • either the target is too noisy for the current setup

  • or the market feature branch is too weak

  • or the selected universe/time span is poorly chosen

  • or evaluation is too strict for the actual sample size

  • or there is a data issue

What failure does not automatically mean

  • it does not automatically prove the whole thesis is impossible

  • it may mean the baseline task setup needs repair before text is introduced

Hard note
If market-only learnability is absent everywhere, you should not jump straight to “news will save it.”
That is usually bad science.

H1b — INCREMENTAL VALUE OF EVENT STATE

Statement
The multimodal model should improve on the market-only baseline, especially on 5-day and 20-day horizons.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • Delta R^2 >= 0.02 on 5-day and 20-day horizons

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    Delta R^2 >= 0.02 on both 5d and 20d, with same-direction benefit across most folds

  • Moderate support:
    Delta R^2 between 0.005 and 0.02, with stable sign across folds and supportive ranking metrics

  • Conditional support:
    weak overall average, but clear gain during high-news-density periods or selected horizons

  • Failure:
    no stable gain over market-only, or gains vanish under paired comparison

What failure would mean

  • event state may not add useful information in the current setup

  • or the text window, pooling, or embedding design is wrong

  • or Finnhub historical coverage is too weak

  • or the market-only branch already absorbs most available signal

Hard note
A tiny average gain with unstable fold behavior is not a core-thesis win.

H2a — STABILITY ACROSS TIME

Statement
The multimodal advantage should not be purely accidental or fold-specific.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • coefficient of variation of Delta R^2 across folds < 0.5

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    CV < 0.5 and positive average delta

  • Weak support:
    CV between 0.5 and 1.0 but sign mostly positive

  • Failure:
    CV > 1.0, sign instability, or one fold driving almost all benefit

What failure would mean

  • regime sensitivity

  • overfit to one period

  • event-state signal exists only under specific conditions

  • or sample size is too small for stable inference

Hard note
An unstable positive average is not the same as a robust result.

H3a — NEWS-DENSITY HETEROGENEITY

Statement
The event-state branch should help more when there is enough news for it to matter.

Existing qualitative and quantitative direction from prior research design

  • largest multimodal advantage in top news-volume quintile

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    top-quintile news-density slices show materially larger delta than low-density slices

  • Weak support:
    benefit appears only in Q4 and Q5 but is small

  • Failure:
    no monotonic relation between news density and multimodal usefulness

What failure would mean

  • event-state branch may be too noisy

  • or article volume is a poor proxy for information relevance

  • or alignment and aggregation are too coarse

Hard note
Conditional usefulness is still a valid thesis result.
It may actually strengthen the story by making it more realistic.

H3b — SECTOR HETEROGENEITY

Statement
Multimodal gains may differ by sector.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • ANOVA p < 0.05 across sectors

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    statistically meaningful sector separation with coherent economic explanation

  • Weak support:
    visible sector patterns but unstable due to small sample counts

  • Failure:
    no interpretable sector structure

Hard note
Do not force this result if sector sample counts are too small.
This is easy to overstate.

H4a — DECAY VS SIMPLE MEAN

Statement
Recency-aware event-state pooling should beat simple averaging.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • Delta R^2 >= 0.01 for exponential decay over simple mean

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    decay beats mean on major horizons with stable fold sign

  • Weak support:
    tiny but consistent advantage on one or two horizons

  • Failure:
    no consistent edge over mean

Hard note
If simple mean is nearly as good, prefer the simpler design for thesis cleanliness.

H4b — DENSE EMBEDDINGS VS SENTIMENT-ONLY

Statement
Dense text representation should beat sentiment-only style inputs.

Existing numeric marker from prior research design

  • Delta R^2 >= 0.01 for dense embeddings over sentiment-only features

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    dense embeddings clearly outperform sentiment-only

  • Weak support:
    small but stable advantage

  • Failure:
    no edge, or sentiment-only is equally good

Hard note
If sentiment-only is equally good, the event-state branch may still matter, but the representation story becomes much weaker.

H4c — LONGER LOOKBACK FOR LONGER HORIZONS

Statement
Longer event-state windows should help longer horizons more than shorter horizons.

Existing directional claim from prior research design

  • longer history, such as 30 days, should help longer horizons more than 7 days

Interpretation bands

  • Strong support:
    30-day lookback helps 20d and maybe 60d, while shorter windows help 1d or 5d more

  • Weak support:
    longer lookback helps modestly but inconsistently

  • Failure:
    no horizon-conditional pattern

Hard note
Do not over-interpret small lookback differences.

<< 23.3 ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLDS FOR METRICS >>

The current repo evaluation layer already supports:

Regression

  • MAE

  • RMSE

  • R^2

  • Pearson

  • Spearman

Classification

  • AUC

  • PR-AUC

  • Brier score

Ranking

  • daily information coefficient

  • ICIR

The old research design also suggested target-like thresholds such as:

  • R^2 > 0.05

  • correlation > 0.15

  • direction accuracy > 52 percent

Use the following practical interpretation bands.

REGRESSION

R^2

  • Strong:

    0.05 at a main horizon

  • Useful but modest:
    0.02 to 0.05

  • Weak:
    0.00 to 0.02

  • Failure:
    <= 0.00

Pearson or Spearman

  • Strong:

    0.15

  • Modest:
    0.05 to 0.15

  • Weak:
    0.01 to 0.05

  • Failure:
    near zero or unstable sign

DIRECTION

Accuracy

  • Strong:

    0.52 with reasonable balance and fold stability

  • Weak:
    0.505 to 0.52

  • Failure:
    about random or unstable

RANKING

Daily IC / ICIR
Because the repo supports daily cross-sectional ranking metrics, these should be treated as first-class secondary evidence, especially if point metrics are small but stable.

Interpretation

  • Strong:
    positive IC with stable sign and nontrivial ICIR

  • Weak:
    positive average IC but unstable

  • Failure:
    inconsistent sign or near-zero average

Important rule
For this thesis, do not let direction accuracy dominate the story.
The project is fundamentally return-oriented and event-state-oriented, not just up/down classification oriented. The README and research design both center forward excess or abnormal returns as the most defensible main target family.

<< 23.4 EXACT STOP/GO RULES BY EXPERIMENT >>

E00 — DATA AND PANEL INTEGRITY

GO if:

  • adjusted-price diagnostics are clean enough to trust labels

  • no major alignment violations

  • no major schema violations

  • final panel remains unique on ticker/date

  • enough rows survive for 1d, 5d, and 20d

STOP if:

  • split windows still create mechanical return spikes

  • article alignment is broken

  • final panel row loss is severe

  • Finnhub coverage is too sparse for text evaluation

E01 — TRIVIAL AND LINEAR BASELINES

GO if:

  • ridge beats constant predictor on at least one main horizon

  • no absurd metric behavior

STOP if:

  • even trivial linear structure cannot beat constant prediction in any meaningful way

E02 — MARKET-ONLY THESIS BASELINE

GO if:

  • at least one market-only model shows nontrivial out-of-sample value

  • folds are not pathological

  • ranking behavior is not contradictory

STOP if:

  • all market-only models fail everywhere

  • all positive signals disappear once purge and embargo are active

E03 — MARKET-ONLY VS MULTIMODAL

GO if:

  • multimodal beats market-only with stable sign on the relevant horizons

  • or conditional gain appears in high-news-density subsets

STOP if:

  • average gain is tiny and unstable

  • gains vanish under paired comparison

  • only one lucky fold creates the whole effect

E04 TO E07 — EVENT-STATE SHAPE

GO if:

  • you can identify one clean default event-state design

  • improvements are interpretable and not just random search artifacts

STOP if:

  • every variant is fragile

  • one choice looks better only because of one fold or one year

E08 — DERIVATIVE FAMILY

GO only if:

  • derivative-like variants still improve after comparison against stronger standard competitors

STOP if:

  • gains vanish when momentum, volatility, range, and volume interaction features are present

  • second-order family is noisy and inconsistent

E11 — STATIC COMPANY BRANCH

GO only if:

  • the core event-state thesis is already supported

  • the metadata branch adds stable value without contaminating comparability

STOP if:

  • it just adds complexity without clear incremental evidence

<< 23.5 FAILURE INTERPRETATION MAP >>

Negative results are not all the same.
Use the following failure map.

CASE A
Market-only fails, multimodal fails

Interpretation

  • the task setup itself may be poorly specified

  • target design, universe design, or time period may be the problem

  • data quality and sample sufficiency must be rechecked

What to do

  • audit target family

  • audit benchmark-relative formulation

  • audit sample size and coverage

  • do not escalate architecture

CASE B
Market-only works, multimodal does not

Interpretation

  • event-state branch may not add information in the current configuration

  • or text coverage, pooling, or representation is weak

  • or market features dominate already

What to do

  • inspect density and regime subgroups

  • inspect event-state design before abandoning the text story completely

CASE C
Multimodal helps only in high-news-density periods

Interpretation

  • strong conditional support for event-state usefulness

  • likely a valid thesis result

  • the correct claim becomes “conditional incremental value,” not “universal value”

CASE D
Multimodal helps on 20d but not 1d

Interpretation

  • coherent with slow information absorption or narrative persistence

  • not a failure

  • actually a strong horizon-specific result

CASE E
Derivative features help only before stronger standard features are added

Interpretation

  • derivative family was redundant

  • likely false sophistication

  • should be demoted or rejected

CASE F
Decay pooling does not beat simple mean

Interpretation

  • recency weighting may be less important than expected

  • the thesis should preserve simplicity instead of forcing a decay story

CASE G
Sector effect appears but is unstable

Interpretation

  • possible real heterogeneity but insufficient evidence

  • keep as exploratory, not definitive

<< 23.7 EXACT WORDING RULES FOR THESIS CLAIMS >>

Use the following wording rules.

If strong support:

  • “improves”

  • “outperforms”

  • “shows robust incremental value”

  • “remains stable across folds”

If weak or conditional support:

  • “shows limited but consistent improvement”

  • “appears most useful under high-news-density conditions”

  • “provides conditional incremental value”

  • “benefits selected horizons”

If failure or non-support:

  • “did not show consistent improvement”

  • “did not outperform the market-only baseline under the chosen protocol”

  • “appeared redundant relative to simpler features”

  • “did not justify the added complexity”

Do not write:

  • “proved”

  • “solved”

  • “significantly better” unless the relevant statistical test truly supports it

  • “state of the art” unless you actually benchmarked that claim properly

<< 23.8 PRACTICAL DEFAULT ACCEPTANCE POLICY >>

If you want one simple operational policy, use this:

CORE SUCCESS

  • market-only shows nontrivial out-of-sample signal

  • multimodal beats market-only on the main horizons with stable sign

  • event-state design is reasonably robust

  • no major integrity failures

PARTIAL SUCCESS

  • multimodal gain is conditional, not universal

  • or only one main horizon benefits

  • or gains are modest but stable

NEGATIVE BUT USEFUL RESULT

  • market-only works

  • multimodal does not improve reliably

  • derivative family is redundant

  • but the study still cleanly establishes what does not work

That last category is still thesis-worthy if the methodology is strong.

<< 23.9 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

The exact thresholds already implied by the project’s prior research design are useful, but they should be treated as strong-success markers, not rigid pass/fail dogma. The current repo and evaluation documents already support a stricter and better framing: frozen datasets, strict temporal integrity, purge/embargo safety, stored-prediction comparison, and one-change-at-a-time ablations. That means the thesis should judge success not only by raw metric size, but by stability, subgroup coherence, comparability discipline, and whether the gain survives against the correct baseline.

The most important practical rule is this:

A small but stable and well-benchmarked gain is more valuable than a larger but fragile one.
And a clean negative result is more valuable than a messy positive illusion.

will be the next continuation block.

<< 24. WHAT THE THESIS SHOULD SAY UNDER EACH POSSIBLE OUTCOME >>

This section is not about spin.
It is about outcome discipline.

The project already has a clear identity:

  • end-of-day

  • multimodal

  • multi-horizon

  • event-state driven

  • return-oriented rather than price-level oriented

  • leakage-aware

  • benchmark-aware

  • academically defensible by design

The repo is also already beyond pure planning. It now contains first-pass end-to-end support for ingestion, split handling, feature generation, event-state construction, final panel assembly, baseline training, first multimodal training, and evaluation/ablations, while the main remaining priorities are documentation hardening, reporting polish, selected multimodal extensions, and manual verification of live provider realities.

That means the thesis must now be prepared for multiple plausible outcomes, not only the optimistic one.

<< 24.1 OUTCOME A — MARKET-ONLY IS STRONG, MULTIMODAL IS STRONGER >>

Observed pattern

  • market-only baseline shows nontrivial out-of-sample signal

  • multimodal model improves on it at one or more main horizons

  • gains remain stable across folds

  • gains survive frozen-label evaluation and stored-prediction comparison

  • subgroup analysis is supportive rather than contradictory

What the thesis should say

<<
The study found that conservative adjusted-price market features already contain measurable out-of-sample predictive signal for multi-horizon excess-return forecasting. More importantly, an aggregated event-state representation derived from recent company news provided incremental predictive value beyond market-only baselines, especially on the horizons where information absorption is less immediate and more semantically cumulative.

What the thesis is allowed to claim

  • event-state modeling adds incremental value beyond market-only baselines

  • the gain is robust under the project’s strict temporal protocol

  • the result supports the event-state framing over purely article-isolated thinking

  • multimodal fusion is justified in this end-of-day setup

What the thesis must still not claim

  • that the model captures causal price impact

  • that the model proves market inefficiency in a broad sense

  • that the result generalizes to all universes, time periods, or data vendors

  • that the architecture is final or state-of-the-art

What this outcome means for future work

  • stronger multimodal architectures become justified extension work

  • static company metadata branch becomes a rational next step

  • uncertainty-aware outputs become worth testing

  • derivative features remain secondary unless they later prove incremental value over the already successful core

How to discuss the derivative idea under Outcome A

If the core multimodal result is already strong, derivative features must justify themselves as incremental additions, not decorative mathematics. They should be presented as:

  • optional feature-family challenge tests

  • not as the reason the project succeeded

Hard criticism

This is the outcome most likely to tempt exaggeration.
Do not let the thesis become:
“news plus market solves stock prediction.”
That would be a weak academic framing and a stronger claim than your setup can support.

<< 24.2 OUTCOME B — MARKET-ONLY IS STRONG, MULTIMODAL IS ONLY CONDITIONALLY BETTER >>

Observed pattern

  • market-only baseline works

  • multimodal average gain is modest or mixed

  • but gains appear clearly in:

    • high-news-density periods

    • certain horizons such as 5d or 20d

    • selected sectors

    • selected regimes

What the thesis should say

<<
The study did not find uniform multimodal improvement across all stock-days and horizons. However, the event-state branch showed conditional incremental value under information-rich conditions, particularly when recent company-news flow was sufficiently dense and when the forecasting horizon allowed delayed semantic information to matter.

This is a very good thesis outcome.
Do not underrate it.

Why this is scientifically strong

Because it is realistic.
The repo’s own research framing already treats event state as an evolving information representation rather than a universal signal that should dominate every date. The project is explicitly designed around the fact that news overlap, narrative evolution, and noisy absorption make universal clean effects unlikely.

What the thesis can claim

  • event-state usefulness is conditional

  • density and horizon matter

  • multimodal value is not constant across contexts

  • benchmark discipline revealed where text matters and where it does not

What the thesis must not claim

  • that text universally improves predictions

  • that weak overall average gains are irrelevant if one subgroup looks good

  • that subgroup results are definitive if sample counts are small

How to present this outcome strongly

Frame it as a structured heterogeneity result:

  • the market branch remains the reliable backbone

  • the event-state branch is a context-dependent enhancer

  • the thesis contribution becomes conditional multimodal usefulness under strict evaluation

How to discuss derivative features under Outcome B

Derivative-like features would only deserve attention if they help explain or improve the same conditional slices.
For example:

  • maybe they help when volatility is high

  • maybe they help on medium horizons

  • maybe they help when news density is high

If they do not reinforce the same conditional structure, they should not be promoted.

Hard criticism

Many theses would hide this outcome because it looks less triumphant than universal improvement.
That would be a mistake.
Conditional usefulness is more believable than universal usefulness in this domain.

<< 24.3 OUTCOME C — MARKET-ONLY IS STRONG, MULTIMODAL DOES NOT IMPROVE RELIABLY >>

Observed pattern

  • market-only baseline produces measurable out-of-sample value

  • multimodal branch is flat, unstable, or only rarely better

  • event-state additions do not survive fold-level scrutiny or paired comparison

What the thesis should say

<<
The study found that conservative market-only models captured the most reliable out-of-sample signal under the chosen data, alignment, and evaluation protocol. The aggregated event-state representation from company news did not produce sufficiently consistent incremental improvement to justify a stronger core claim of multimodal advantage.

This is still a valid thesis result.

Why this is not a failure in the academic sense

Because the project is not only about finding a winner.
It is also about establishing:

  • a defensible benchmark framework

  • a leakage-safe multimodal pipeline

  • a falsifiable event-state test

  • and a disciplined answer to whether the text branch truly helps

A clean null result is better than a fragile positive one.

What this outcome may imply

  • company-news coverage is too sparse or too noisy

  • the event-state aggregation rule is too crude

  • the chosen embedding family is not strong enough

  • the market-only branch already absorbs most usable EOD signal

  • or the information in headlines is not sufficiently incremental in this setup

What the thesis can claim

  • the event-state hypothesis was meaningfully tested

  • the market branch is the reliable foundation

  • more complexity was not automatically better

  • rigorous evaluation prevented overclaiming

What the thesis must not do

  • blame the null result on vague “lack of compute”

  • suddenly change targets and architectures at the end just to rescue a positive story

  • pretend that small unstable gains are meaningful

How to discuss derivative features under Outcome C

Under this outcome, derivative-style market features become even more suspect as a rescue strategy.
If text did not help, the thesis should not jump into feature proliferation unless there is a precise reason.
A derivative family could still be tested, but only as:

  • a narrow extension

  • not as a narrative replacement for the missing multimodal signal

Hard criticism

This is the outcome where many projects become dishonest.
They start changing windows, targets, and metrics until something turns positive.
Do not do that.

<< 24.4 OUTCOME D — BOTH MARKET-ONLY AND MULTIMODAL ARE WEAK >>

Observed pattern

  • baselines are near-zero or unstable

  • multimodal branch does not rescue them

  • ranking metrics are also weak

  • fold behavior is noisy

  • subgroup slicing does not produce a coherent story

What the thesis should say

<<
Under the selected universe, target construction, data sources, and evaluation protocol, the study did not find sufficiently reliable out-of-sample predictive structure to support stronger claims about either market-only or event-state-driven multimodal forecasting. This result suggests that the key challenge is not merely architecture choice, but task formulation, data quality, and the practical limits of the available information sources.

This is the harshest outcome, but it is still usable if handled honestly.

What this likely means

  • target design may be too noisy

  • excess-return formulation may need revision

  • universe may be too broad or too sparse

  • Finnhub historical coverage may be insufficient

  • the time period may not suit the intended hypothesis

  • or the evaluation setup is revealing that the problem is harder than initially assumed

What to do academically

Convert the thesis emphasis from “successful forecasting system” to:

  • methodological audit

  • benchmark framework

  • negative result with diagnosis

  • identified failure modes and repair directions

What the thesis can still contribute

  • a clean end-to-end architecture

  • split-safe and leakage-safe financial ML pipeline design

  • evidence about where common optimism breaks down

  • a disciplined map of what should be changed next

What the thesis must not do

  • claim hidden success from one lucky fold

  • replace rigorous out-of-sample evaluation with anecdotal examples

  • treat implementation completeness as equivalent to empirical success

How to discuss derivative features under Outcome D

In this outcome, the derivative idea should almost certainly be demoted.
If the core task is not showing reliable learnability, derivative proliferation is more likely to create false positives than real progress.

Hard criticism

If both branches are weak, the next step is not “deeper model.”
It is “better problem specification.”

<< 24.5 OUTCOME E — DERIVATIVE FEATURES SHOW REAL INCREMENTAL VALUE >>

Observed pattern

  • derivative-like market features improve on the already strong simpler market feature set

  • gains survive against returns, momentum, volatility, range, and volume interactions

  • results are stable and interpretable

  • benefits are especially coherent at specific horizons

What the thesis should say

<<
A narrow family of derivative-like market transforms produced incremental value beyond the conservative standard feature set. Their usefulness appears to stem not from mathematical novelty alone, but from their ability to capture changes in local market motion that interact meaningfully with the event-state framing.

Important wording:
narrow family

Do not say:
“derivatives of OHLCV are the key innovation”
unless the evidence is unusually strong.

What would make this outcome believable

  • normalized first-order transforms beat simpler competitors

  • maybe rolling slope or smoothed curvature proxies help

  • second-order raw-difference noise does not dominate the story

  • gains are not just one-window luck

How to keep this academically clean

Present the derivative family as:

  • a disciplined extension finding

  • subordinate to the main market-vs-event-state benchmark ladder

  • and not as a late-stage gimmick

Hard criticism

Even in this optimistic derivative outcome, you should still suspect redundancy first.
Only promote the feature family if it clearly survives comparison with the stronger standard alternatives.

<< 24.6 OUTCOME F — DERIVATIVE FEATURES LOOK GOOD EARLY BUT COLLAPSE UNDER FAIR COMPARISON >>

Observed pattern

  • derivative variants initially seem promising

  • but gains disappear once you add:

    • momentum

    • volatility

    • range

    • volume surprise

    • rolling slope

  • second-order variants are unstable or fold-fragile

What the thesis should say

<<
Derivative-like market transforms were investigated as a possible extension feature family. While some early variants appeared promising, their advantage did not survive comparison against stronger and more standard market feature families. The evidence therefore suggests that these transforms were largely redundant or too noise-sensitive to justify a core role.

This would be a strong and useful negative result.

Why it matters

Because the derivative idea is exactly the kind of proposal that can waste time if not criticized hard.
A rigorous rejection is intellectually valuable.

What the thesis can claim

  • the derivative idea was tested fairly

  • it was not simply ignored

  • simpler and more standard feature families dominated it

  • false sophistication was avoided

What this does for the thesis

It strengthens the project’s credibility.
It shows the thesis could reject an attractive internal idea rather than preserving it for elegance.

<< 24.7 OUTCOME G — SIMPLE EVENT-STATE DESIGN BEATS MORE COMPLEX VARIANTS >>

Observed pattern

  • simple mean or exponential decay pooling works

  • more complex alternatives do not help enough

  • frozen embeddings are sufficient

  • attention-style or richer multimodal routing does not justify complexity

What the thesis should say

<<
The study found that a simple and well-controlled event-state design was sufficient for the strongest reproducible results obtained in this setting. More complex multimodal alternatives did not provide enough additional value to justify their benchmarking burden or interpretability cost.

This is a very strong thesis outcome.

Why

Because the repo and roadmap explicitly prioritize:

  • correctness

  • reproducibility

  • leakage safety

  • and only then modeling sophistication

This outcome would show the project followed that principle successfully.

<< 24.8 OUTCOME H — COMPANY METADATA HELPS ONLY SLIGHTLY >>

Observed pattern

  • static company metadata gives small gains

  • gains are stable but modest

  • the core event-state result remains dominant

What the thesis should say

<<
Static company metadata provided a modest but consistent complement to the main multimodal setup. However, its contribution remained secondary to the central market-plus-event-state comparison, and time-varying profile extensions were intentionally left outside the core claim due to their greater leakage sensitivity.

This is likely the cleanest way to treat the company branch if you reach it.

Why this matches the repo

The current architecture explicitly treats the company-profile branch as not yet wired into training and as a later architectural priority, not as the first proof point.

<< 24.9 OUTCOME I — REPORTING AND METHODOLOGICAL CONTRIBUTION MATTER MORE THAN THE FINAL METRIC >>

There is another valid thesis outcome that students often underuse.

Observed pattern

  • results are mixed or moderate

  • but the pipeline, evaluation rigor, benchmark structure, and anti-leakage design are strong

  • the repo now genuinely embodies a careful experimental framework

What the thesis should say

<<
A major contribution of the project is methodological rather than purely metric. The work establishes a reproducible and leakage-aware end-to-end framework for event-state-driven multimodal financial forecasting, with explicit split handling, strict as-of-close alignment, frozen final panels, and comparable ablation procedures. This framework provides a stronger basis for future financial ML experiments than ad hoc benchmark practice.

This is not a consolation prize.
It is a real contribution if written honestly and supported properly.

It is especially defensible because the repo now really does include:

  • explicit data contracts

  • separate raw/interim/final layering

  • split-adjusted branch handling

  • alignment rules

  • walk-forward and purged/embargoed validation

  • stored-prediction evaluation

  • ablation support

<< 24.10 THESIS CONCLUSION LANGUAGE BY OUTCOME >>

Use these sentence families directly.

If Outcome A

<<
The evidence supports the main project hypothesis: under a strict end-of-day and leakage-aware protocol, aggregated event-state features from recent company news provide incremental value beyond market-only baselines for multi-horizon excess-return forecasting.

If Outcome B

<<
The evidence supports a conditional version of the main hypothesis: event-state features are most useful under information-rich conditions and are not uniformly beneficial across all stock-days or horizons.

If Outcome C

<<
The evidence does not support a broad claim of multimodal advantage in the current setup. The strongest and most reliable performance came from the conservative market-only branch.

If Outcome D

<<
The evidence does not support strong forecasting claims under the chosen setup, suggesting that task formulation, data realism, and source limitations matter more here than additional modeling complexity.

If derivative family is supported narrowly

<<
A narrow derivative-like feature family appears worth retaining as a secondary extension, but not as the defining core of the project.

If derivative family is rejected

<<
Derivative-like market transforms did not justify a core role once compared fairly against stronger standard feature families.

<< 24.11 WHAT MUST BE PRESERVED NO MATTER THE OUTCOME >>

Regardless of which outcome occurs, the thesis should preserve these elements as permanent assets:

  • strict end-of-day identity

  • event-state framing instead of article-level causal storytelling

  • adjusted-price requirement

  • frozen raw/interim/final layering

  • canonical data contracts

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • walk-forward with purge and embargo

  • saved-prediction evaluation

  • one-change-at-a-time ablations

  • refusal to equate more complexity with better science

Those are not optional style choices.
They are the project’s backbone, and the repo already encodes them across the current architecture, data layout, evaluation protocol, execution plan, and current README.

<< 24.12 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

The thesis should never be written as if only one outcome is acceptable.
That mindset causes p-hacking, architecture drift, and weak academic honesty.

A strong thesis from this project is not defined only by whether multimodal wins.
It is defined by whether the project can say, truthfully and cleanly, one of the following:

  • the event-state branch adds robust value

  • the event-state branch adds conditional value

  • the event-state branch does not justify itself in the current setup

  • derivative features are helpful only narrowly

  • derivative features are redundant

  • careful benchmark design matters more than seductive feature or architecture inflation

That is the correct scientific posture for the restart.

<< 25. WHAT SHOULD BE STABILIZED BEFORE THE FIRST SERIOUS THESIS RUN, AND WHAT SHOULD STILL BE POSTPONED EVEN IF YOU ARE TEMPTED >>
is the next continuation block.

<< 25. WHAT SHOULD BE STABILIZED BEFORE THE FIRST SERIOUS THESIS RUN, AND WHAT SHOULD STILL BE POSTPONED EVEN IF YOU ARE TEMPTED >>

This section matters because the repository is no longer in pure design mode.
It is already in late foundation / early experimentation.
The core pipeline layers now exist:

  • ingestion

  • split handling

  • features

  • event state

  • final panel assembly

  • market-only training

  • first multimodal training

  • evaluation and ablation tooling

The repo’s own current documents therefore imply a very specific research posture:
do not widen scope carelessly now.
Stabilize the benchmark foundation first.
Then run the first serious thesis wave.
Only after that should selected extensions be allowed.

<< 25.1 WHAT COUNTS AS THE FIRST SERIOUS THESIS RUN >>

A serious thesis run is not:

  • a smoke test

  • a pilot just to see whether the code executes

  • a one-split result

  • a quick hashing-backend sanity check

  • an experiment where the dataset definition is still moving

A serious thesis run is:

  • based on a frozen dataset family

  • based on a frozen universe file

  • based on a frozen benchmark choice

  • based on frozen target definitions

  • based on the official as-of-close alignment policy

  • based on adjusted prices from an auditable split source

  • based on saved predictions and frozen labels

  • based on walk-forward plus purge and embargo

  • and reported in a way that another researcher could rerun and compare fairly

That definition is already consistent with the current architecture, data layout, evaluation protocol, and execution plan. The project is explicitly structured around raw/interim/final separation, adjusted-price integrity, frozen final panels, and stored-prediction evaluation rather than informal notebook claims.

<< 25.2 WHAT MUST BE STABILIZED BEFORE THAT RUN >>

The following items should be treated as non-negotiable preconditions.

A. ONE CANONICAL UNIVERSE DEFINITION

You must freeze:

  • exact ticker list

  • exact universe file path

  • exact inclusion rationale

  • exact benchmark ticker

The execution flow already warns against jumping straight to the full 503-name live universe and instead recommends starting from pilot10 and then moving to a curated 30 to 100 stock subset for serious experiments. That is the correct discipline. A moving universe destroys comparability unless it is explicitly treated as a new benchmark family.

My recommendation:
for the first serious thesis run, freeze one curated experiment file, such as experiment50 or experiment100, and do not keep changing names between baseline and multimodal phases.

B. ONE CANONICAL SPLIT SOURCE POLICY

This is one of the most important stabilization points in the whole project.

Before a serious run, you must freeze:

  • which split-event source is being used

  • whether fallback data is allowed

  • what missing-split policy applies

  • how split-adjustment diagnostics are documented

The repo is explicit that raw and adjusted prices are separate branches, that split events are canonical interim tables, and that adjusted prices are generated locally rather than by silently trusting provider-side adjustment behavior. The execution flow also states that direct split-event generation now exists, often using Twelve Data when available and yfinance fallback otherwise, but that this must be documented clearly in research outputs.

My direct warning:
If you change split source midway through the benchmark ladder, your labels are no longer meaningfully comparable.

C. ONE OFFICIAL ARTICLE ALIGNMENT RULE

You must freeze:

  • timezone normalization

  • market-close cutoff rule

  • after-hours rollover rule

  • non-trading-day rollover rule

  • whether embargo is used only at split generation or also at feature construction

The current evaluation protocol already defines the official policy:
only articles available by the market close on date t may be used for date t; after-hours and non-trading-day articles roll to the next valid trading day. The architecture also explicitly requires alignment logic to remain centralized in src/split/alignment_rules.py.

My criticism of earlier project thinking:
Any lingering ambiguity here is fatal.
If the alignment rule is not frozen, the text branch is scientifically unstable.

D. ONE CANONICAL TEXT VARIANT

Before the serious run, freeze:

  • headline only
    or

  • headline plus summary

Do not alternate variants across model families inside the same benchmark family.

Why this matters:
the embedding cache and event-state branch are built on canonical article text and text hashes. If you change the text variant, you have changed the representation family, not merely tuned a hyperparameter. The current implementation already tracks text variants explicitly.

My recommendation:
use headline plus summary when available, because that is already the repo’s natural first-pass direction.
But freeze it once chosen.

E. ONE CANONICAL EMBEDDING BACKEND FOR THE THESIS CORE

The execution flow explicitly recommends:

  • hashing backend first for fast validation

  • real sentence-transformer embeddings for serious experiments later

That means:

  • hashing is acceptable for smoke tests

  • hashing is not the right basis for the first real thesis claim unless you intentionally frame the run as a systems-validation baseline

My recommendation:
freeze one real dense embedding model for the first serious thesis run.
Do not compare market-only against hashing multimodal and then compare stronger multimodal variants with a different encoder unless you clearly mark that as a new benchmark family.

F. ONE CANONICAL EVENT-STATE DEFAULT

Before the serious run, freeze:

  • one lookback

  • one decay rule

  • one no-news policy

  • one set of scalar extras such as density or novelty if included

The old research design already proposes a natural first default:

  • 30-day lookback

  • 7-day half-life

  • event-state aggregation from dense embeddings

  • density-aware interpretation as a subgroup lens rather than necessarily a required feature.

My recommendation:
for the first serious thesis run, use exactly one default event-state design and reserve all alternatives for later ablations.

G. ONE CANONICAL TARGET FAMILY

This should already be familiar by now:
freeze one primary target family before the serious run.

The strongest current choice remains:

  • multi-horizon excess returns
    with horizons like

  • 1d

  • 5d

  • 20d
    and maybe 60d only if sample coverage and stability remain acceptable. This is consistent with the current README, research design, and feature/label logic.

My recommendation:
1d, 5d, and 20d should be the serious core.
60d is extension territory unless the rest of the setup is already stable.

H. ONE CANONICAL FOLD POLICY

The evaluation protocol already states that all evaluation must be strictly out-of-sample in time, label overlap must be handled explicitly, and final reported comparisons should be based on frozen datasets and stored predictions. It also states that the current split builder supports walk-forward chronology plus horizon-aware purge and optional embargo.

Before the serious run, freeze:

  • expanding vs rolling walk-forward

  • train window

  • validation window

  • test window

  • max horizon used to determine purge

  • embargo setting

  • whether validation slices are always used

Do not tune the split policy to favor a model.

I. ONE CANONICAL REPORTING PACKET

Before the serious run, decide exactly what every run must save:

  • resolved configs

  • dataset version

  • model family

  • fold definitions

  • predictions

  • metrics

  • run metadata

  • training summary

  • comparison summary

This is already aligned with the execution flow and architecture boundary that evaluation should operate on saved predictions and frozen labels, not notebook state.

If a run cannot produce a reproducible packet, it should not count as a thesis result.

<< 25.3 WHAT SHOULD BE MANUALLY VERIFIED BEFORE THE FIRST SERIOUS RUN >>

The repo is clear that some things remain implemented but not yet fully externally verified:

  • live provider behavior

  • split-source reality on the active market-data plan

  • live Finnhub historical completeness

  • practical runtime behavior under real quotas

That means the following manual checks are required before thesis-strength claims:

  1. Verify split windows on several known names
    Examples:

  • AAPL 2020-08-31

  • TSLA 2020-08-31

  • NVDA 2021-07-20

  1. Verify benchmark coverage and date alignment
    The serious run should not silently drop dates because benchmark data is missing.

  2. Verify Finnhub coverage for the exact historical window you intend to use
    The execution flow already warns that zero articles over a chosen range does not necessarily mean pipeline failure; it may reflect plan limitations or historical incompleteness.

  3. Verify dot tickers through the full path
    This includes at least:

  • BRK.B

  • BF.B

  1. Verify no-news handling
    You must know whether no-news days are:

  • encoded as zero vector

  • encoded as missing

  • excluded
    Changing this later changes the feature branch definition.

<< 25.4 WHAT SHOULD STILL BE POSTPONED EVEN IF YOU ARE TEMPTED >>

Now the hard part.

There are several things that will feel attractive at this stage because the repo is already capable enough to attempt them.
Some of them are reasonable later.
Some of them are mostly temptation.

A. DO NOT PROMOTE THE DERIVATIVE FAMILY TO CORE BEFORE THE CORE BENCHMARK IS STABLE

This deserves blunt wording.

Your derivative idea is still not core.
It is still an extension candidate.
Even if you like it intellectually, it should not be allowed to redefine the first serious thesis run.

Why:

  • the serious run must first answer whether market plus event state beats market-only

  • derivative experiments multiply feature-space freedom

  • they are especially vulnerable to window shopping

  • many of them are redundant with simpler motion families

So even if tempted:
postpone derivative-family expansion until the core benchmark ladder is frozen and working.

B. DO NOT ADD END-TO-END TEXT FINE-TUNING

The implementation roadmap explicitly says not to add end-to-end text fine-tuning before baseline and multimodal comparisons are stable. The README and architecture also treat frozen embedding pipelines as the intended early research regime.

Why this must stay postponed:

  • harder to reproduce

  • harder to benchmark fairly

  • much higher compute and debugging burden

  • harder to know whether gains come from representation or leakage-like preprocessing asymmetries

C. DO NOT ADD TIME-VARYING COMPANY PROFILE BRANCHES YET

The implementation roadmap explicitly warns not to add time-varying profile branches before a clear leakage-safe design exists. The README also says static identity and metadata should come first, with time-varying descriptive profile branches postponed.

Why this must stay postponed:

  • timestamp safety is hard

  • profile text is leakage-prone

  • it adds another modality before the main one is proven

  • it complicates ablation logic

D. DO NOT ADD GRAPH, RELATION-AWARE, OR MOE SYSTEMS YET

These ideas are attractive because they sound like “real research.”
But at this stage they would likely be architecture inflation.

Why postpone:

  • the current multimodal model is intentionally simple

  • the architecture overview explicitly lists more advanced multimodal ablations only after current results are stable and reproducible

  • richer multimodal extensions are listed as later priorities, not immediate necessities

My criticism:
A graph or expert-routing branch before a strong baseline map exists is usually a sign that the project is chasing novelty before it has locked down truth.

E. DO NOT EXPAND TARGETS CASUALLY

Do not, before the first serious run, add all of the following at once:

  • raw returns

  • excess returns

  • abnormal returns

  • direction labels

  • downside labels

  • quantiles

  • uncertainty heads

Choose one primary target family.
Keep secondary targets secondary.

If you change target family midstream, you are not merely enriching the experiment.
You are moving the problem definition.

F. DO NOT JUMP TO THE FULL 503-NAME LIVE UNIVERSE

The execution flow is very clear about this:
do not jump straight to full 503-name live runs before validating a smaller real-data subset, especially under Twelve Data Basic and plan-dependent Finnhub throughput.

Why postpone:

  • quota pressure

  • runtime uncertainty

  • larger operational failure surface

  • more difficult debugging

  • stronger temptation to accept partial data silently

My recommendation:
serious thesis run first on a curated 30 to 100 stock universe.
Only after that, consider larger-scale replication.

G. DO NOT OVERCOMPLICATE EVALUATION BEFORE STORED-PREDICTION COMPARISON IS FULLY TRUSTED

This is also explicitly stated in the roadmap.

That means:

  • no giant reporting stack first

  • no elaborate presentation polish before the predictions themselves are trusted

  • no fancy figures compensating for unstable evidence

You need trustworthy saved predictions first.
Then richer report generation.

H. DO NOT KEEP CHANGING “SMALL” PREPROCESSING DETAILS

At this stage, the following are not small:

  • text variant

  • no-news encoding

  • benchmark choice

  • split source

  • horizon set

  • event-state lookback

  • event-state decay

  • training split sizes

Changing any of these during the serious run period creates benchmark drift.

<< 25.5 WHAT TO DO INSTEAD OF THESE TEMPTATIONS >>

If you feel tempted to widen scope, do one of these instead:

Instead of derivative-feature expansion:

  • freeze the baseline market feature set

  • add one small derivative-family appendix experiment later

Instead of end-to-end text fine-tuning:

  • test one stronger frozen embedding model

  • keep encoder frozen

Instead of time-varying profile branch:

  • add a tiny static company metadata branch only after core multimodal evidence exists

Instead of graph or MoE:

  • improve subgroup analysis

  • improve fold stability analysis

  • improve paired comparison reporting

Instead of moving to 503 names:

  • run one replicated serious experiment on a second curated subset

  • or run the same frozen benchmark family on a later date range

Instead of many targets:

  • run one target family well

  • then test one secondary target as a clearly separate extension

<< 25.6 EXACT STABILIZATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THE FIRST SERIOUS RUN >>

Use this as a gate.

A serious run should not begin until all items below are true:

DATA FOUNDATION

  • one frozen universe file exists

  • benchmark ticker is frozen

  • split-event source is frozen

  • adjusted prices are generated and audited

  • Finnhub history for the chosen window is confirmed usable

  • no critical schema validation issues remain

FEATURE FOUNDATION

  • text variant is frozen

  • embedding backend is frozen

  • event-state default is frozen

  • no-news behavior is frozen

  • market feature family is frozen

  • target family is frozen

EVALUATION FOUNDATION

  • walk-forward policy is frozen

  • purge and embargo policy is frozen

  • saved-prediction evaluation path is working

  • fold summaries are reproducible

  • paired comparison path is working

  • subgroup slicing logic is ready

ARTIFACT FOUNDATION

  • final panel is versioned

  • manifest is written

  • run metadata is saved

  • predictions are exportable

  • metrics are exportable

  • run-to-dataset traceability is preserved

DOCUMENTATION FOUNDATION

  • README is aligned with actual code

  • guidebook is not materially stale

  • evaluation protocol reflects actual current behavior

  • execution flow reflects actual current CLIs and current missing CLIs

All of these are consistent with the repo’s own stated remaining priorities of documentation hardening, reporting polish, and manual external verification before later-stage extensions are treated as serious.

<< 25.7 WHAT SHOULD BE CLASSIFIED AS CORE NOW, LATER, OR NOT YET >>

CORE BEFORE THE FIRST SERIOUS RUN

  • fixed curated universe

  • explicit split-safe adjusted prices

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • conservative market features

  • frozen dense embedding pipeline

  • one default event-state design

  • excess-return multi-horizon labels

  • walk-forward with purge and embargo

  • market-only vs multimodal comparison

  • saved-prediction evaluation

  • density and horizon subgroup analysis

LATER, AFTER THE FIRST SERIOUS RUN

  • derivative-family appendix tests

  • static company metadata branch

  • stronger report-generation layer

  • broader statistical comparison suite

  • one stronger frozen embedding-family comparison

NOT YET

  • end-to-end text fine-tuning

  • time-varying profile branch

  • graph/relation-aware systems

  • mixture-of-experts

  • giant target zoo

  • full-universe live runs as the first thesis benchmark

  • attention-heavy fusion as a new default

<< 25.8 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

Before the first serious thesis run, the project should not try to become more ambitious.
It should try to become less movable.

That is the real lesson of the current repo state.

The codebase is already strong enough for pilot experiments and methodological validation, but its own current documents say the remaining priorities are documentation hardening, richer reporting, selected extensions, and manual provider verification. That means the right next move is stabilization, not expansion.

The most important practical rule is this:

Freeze the benchmark family before you chase the next clever idea.

And the most important “do not do this yet” rule is this:

Do not let derivative features, richer multimodal architectures, or profile branches hijack the first serious thesis run.

<< 26. THE ACTUAL STAGED RESEARCH PLAN FROM HERE: FIRST SERIOUS RUN, SECOND WAVE, EXTENSION WAVE, AND FINAL THESIS ASSEMBLY >>

This section converts everything above into the actual research sequence that should govern the project from this point forward.

The repo is no longer a concept skeleton. It now contains a coherent first-pass end-to-end system spanning data ingestion, split adjustment, news alignment, event-state construction, final panel assembly, baseline training, first multimodal training, and stored-prediction evaluation. The current remaining priorities in the repo’s own documents are documentation hardening, richer reporting, selected extensions, and manual external verification, not a chaotic expansion of architecture families.

So the correct plan now is not “keep exploring.”
It is:

  • freeze the benchmark basis,

  • run the first serious thesis wave,

  • only then run the controlled second wave,

  • then a small extension wave,

  • and only after that assemble the thesis narrative.

<< 26.1 OVERALL PHASE MAP >>

Use exactly four research phases from here:

PHASE A

  • First serious thesis run

PHASE B

  • Second wave: core event-state and robustness analysis

PHASE C

  • Extension wave: controlled late additions only

PHASE D

  • Final thesis assembly and claims discipline

This phase order is fully consistent with:

  • the current late-foundation / early-experimentation state in the README,

  • the implementation roadmap stating that pilot experimentation is now possible,

  • the execution flow recommending a smaller serious experiment set before any full-universe escalation,

  • and the architecture overview emphasizing that richer multimodal variants come only after stable and reproducible current results.

<< 26.2 PHASE A — FIRST SERIOUS THESIS RUN >>

Primary purpose

The purpose of Phase A is not to optimize everything.
It is to answer the core thesis question once under frozen, serious conditions:

Does event-state-driven multimodal forecasting add value beyond the market-only benchmark under a leakage-aware end-of-day protocol?

That is the main research question already formalized in the research design.

<< 26.2.1 What Phase A must freeze >>

Before Phase A begins, freeze all of the following:

  • one serious universe file

  • one benchmark series

  • one split-event source policy

  • one adjusted-price policy

  • one text variant

  • one embedding backend

  • one event-state default

  • one horizon set

  • one fold policy

  • one primary metric family

  • one reporting packet format

The data layout and evaluation protocol already assume stable canonical tables, manifests, frozen datasets, and saved-prediction evaluation. If these are not frozen, Phase A is not a serious run.

<< 26.2.2 Recommended Phase A defaults >>

Use the following defaults unless direct repository evidence or live verification forces a different choice:

  • universe:
    one curated 30 to 100 stock experiment file

  • benchmark:
    one broad market benchmark only

  • targets:
    excess returns at 1d, 5d, and 20d

  • prices:
    locally split-adjusted only

  • text:
    headline plus summary

  • embeddings:
    one frozen dense sentence embedding model

  • event-state:
    30-day lookback
    exponential decay
    7-day half-life

  • folds:
    walk-forward with purge and optional embargo

  • baselines:
    constant
    ridge
    one market-only neural baseline

  • main multimodal:
    first-pass gated market plus event-state regressor

These defaults are directly aligned with the repo’s current research framing, execution flow, and old research design: excess returns are the recommended primary target family, event state is aggregated over recent news, multi-horizon evaluation is central, and the first multimodal model is intentionally simple rather than over-engineered.

<< 26.2.3 Exact Phase A experiment set >>

Phase A should contain only these serious experiments:

A1

  • Dataset integrity and split-audit freeze

A2

  • Constant baseline

  • OLS or ridge baseline

  • optional elastic net if already supported cleanly

A3

  • Market-only thesis baseline

  • one official market-only benchmark selected

A4

  • Main multimodal comparison

  • market-only versus event-state multimodal

A5

  • News-density subgroup analysis

A6

  • Time-period stability analysis

That is enough.
Anything beyond that belongs to Phase B or later.

<< 26.2.4 What Phase A should output >>

At the end of Phase A, you should have exactly this evidence set:

  • one frozen dataset version

  • one main baseline comparison table

  • one fold-stability table

  • one density subgroup table

  • one time-period stability table

  • one paired comparison summary

  • one written go / partial-go / no-go interpretation

If Phase A finishes without those outputs, then the problem is still in systems-debugging mode, not thesis-evidence mode.

<< 26.2.5 How to interpret Phase A outcomes >>

If Phase A shows:

  • strong market-only

  • stable multimodal improvement

then the core thesis is alive.

If Phase A shows:

  • strong market-only

  • weak but conditional multimodal gain

then the thesis should proceed under a conditional usefulness framing.

If Phase A shows:

  • strong market-only

  • no reliable multimodal gain

then the thesis continues, but the event-state claim must become weaker and more diagnostic.

If Phase A shows:

  • weak market-only

  • weak multimodal

then the next step is not architecture inflation.
It is problem reformulation and data realism review.

<< 26.3 PHASE B — SECOND WAVE: CORE EVENT-STATE AND ROBUSTNESS ANALYSIS >>

Primary purpose

Phase B begins only after Phase A has produced interpretable serious results.

Its job is to answer:

What exactly about the event-state branch matters, how stable is it, and where does it help?

This is where you begin careful model-family understanding.
Not before.

<< 26.3.1 Phase B scope >>

Phase B should contain only the following controlled families:

B1

  • event-state aggregation ablation

    • simple mean

    • exponential decay

    • linear decay if desired

B2

  • lookback ablation

    • 7d

    • 14d

    • 30d

B3

  • representation ablation

    • dense embeddings

    • sentiment-only proxy or coarser text representation if implemented

B4

  • multi-horizon versus single-horizon comparison

B5

  • sector heterogeneity
    only if sector counts are large enough to interpret

B6

  • stronger year-by-year or regime-like stability analysis

These are the natural Phase B topics because they directly refine the core event-state thesis without redefining the whole project. They are also supported by the prior research design hypotheses and the current evaluation/ablation logic.

<< 26.3.2 What Phase B must not do >>

Phase B must not:

  • change the universe

  • change the split source

  • change the target family

  • change the benchmark series

  • switch to end-to-end text training

  • add company-profile branches yet

  • introduce derivative-feature proliferation yet

If any of those happen, you are no longer refining the core event-state claim.
You are changing the benchmark family.

<< 26.3.3 What Phase B should produce >>

At the end of Phase B, you should know:

  • whether recency weighting really matters

  • whether longer lookback helps longer horizons

  • whether dense semantics matter beyond coarse text signals

  • whether multi-task training helps or hurts

  • whether event-state usefulness is robust or conditional

This is the stage that turns the project from:
“we built a multimodal model”
into
“we understand what kind of multimodal signal exists here.”

<< 26.4 PHASE C — EXTENSION WAVE: CONTROLLED LATE ADDITIONS ONLY >>

Primary purpose

Phase C exists for carefully selected additions that are scientifically interesting but not core to proving the thesis foundation.

Phase C should happen only if:

  • Phase A was interpretable
    and

  • Phase B produced a stable enough understanding of the event-state branch

The repo’s current documents explicitly frame richer multimodal architectures, optional company-profile support, uncertainty-aware outputs, and stronger ablations as later-stage research extensions, not immediate priorities.

<< 26.4.1 Allowed Phase C families >>

Only the following kinds of work belong here:

C1

  • derivative-family challenge test

  • static company metadata branch

  • one stronger frozen embedding model comparison

  • one richer reporting and statistical layer

  • optional uncertainty-aware prediction outputs

  • one narrow improved multimodal fusion variant
    only if Phase A and Phase B justified it

<< 26.4.2 Where the derivative idea belongs >>

This is the direct answer to your proposal in sequencing terms:

The derivative idea belongs in Phase C.
Not in Phase A.
Not at the start of Phase B.

Why:

  • it is not required to answer the main multimodal research question

  • it competes with simpler market feature families that should already be present

  • it is vulnerable to window-grid overreach

  • it can easily become false sophistication if tested too early

That means the right formulation is:

“After the core market-only versus event-state thesis benchmark is stabilized, test whether a narrow family of derivative-like transforms adds incremental signal beyond the conservative market feature set.”

That is the defensible way to study it.

<< 26.4.3 Exact derivative test policy in Phase C >>

When Phase C begins, the derivative-family test should be narrow:

Allowed:

  • first-order normalized transforms

  • rolling slope style features

  • one small second-order family if carefully justified

  • only a few windows:
    1d, 5d, 10d, 20d, maybe 30d

Not allowed:

  • dozens of windows

  • raw unnormalized derivative explosion

  • treating derivative features as a new thesis core

  • comparing derivative-augmented models only against weak baselines

The comparison set must always include:

  • returns

  • log returns

  • momentum

  • volatility

  • range

  • volume surprise

  • benchmark-relative context

If derivatives do not survive against those, they should be demoted or rejected.

<< 26.4.4 Static company metadata branch timing >>

A static company metadata branch can also belong in Phase C.

Why it belongs later:

  • the architecture overview explicitly states the company-profile branch is not yet wired into training

  • the README treats it as a useful extension, not the first proof point

  • it is less central than the event-state question for the current core thesis framing

So the correct order is:

  • prove market plus event-state first

  • then test whether static company metadata adds a small stable increment

<< 26.5 PHASE D — FINAL THESIS ASSEMBLY >>

Primary purpose

Phase D is where the research becomes a thesis document rather than a repository story.

This phase should begin only after:

  • the core claim family is clear

  • the benchmark family is frozen

  • the extension results are classified properly

  • the project knows which claims are strong, conditional, weak, or rejected

<< 26.5.1 What Phase D must assemble >>

Phase D should produce the final thesis around five evidence layers:

LAYER 1

  • problem framing

  • why price-level prediction was rejected

  • why event state is the right conceptual lens

LAYER 2

  • system and data architecture

  • raw/interim/final layering

  • split handling

  • alignment policy

  • leakage control

LAYER 3

  • baseline ladder

  • why market-only comes first

  • what constitutes fair multimodal comparison

LAYER 4

  • main empirical findings

  • market-only versus multimodal

  • stability

  • heterogeneity

  • ablations

LAYER 5

  • extension findings and rejected ideas

  • derivative-family outcome

  • static metadata outcome

  • what was postponed and why

The repo’s current README, architecture, data layout, evaluation protocol, and implementation roadmap already contain the raw material for Layers 1 through 4; Phase D’s job is to turn them into a coherent academic narrative without overclaiming.

<< 26.5.2 What Phase D must not do >>

Phase D must not:

  • pretend a late extension caused the main result if it did not

  • hide negative or conditional findings

  • blur the line between core and extension

  • treat pilot runs as final thesis evidence

  • ignore provider limitations that shaped data availability

  • turn engineering completeness into empirical proof

<< 26.5.3 Required thesis chapter logic >>

A strong final thesis sequence would look like this:

Chapter 1

  • problem framing and research questions

Chapter 2

  • literature and conceptual map

  • event-state framing

  • multimodal finance

  • leakage-aware forecasting

Chapter 3

  • data architecture and methodology

  • universe

  • market data

  • news data

  • split adjustment

  • alignment

  • features

  • labels

  • evaluation protocol

Chapter 4

  • baseline and main empirical results

  • market-only

  • multimodal

  • stability

  • density and horizon analyses

Chapter 5

  • controlled ablations and extensions

  • event-state variants

  • derivative-family test

  • optional metadata branch

  • rejected or postponed directions

Chapter 6

  • conclusion

  • what was established

  • what remained conditional

  • what should be done next

<< 26.6 EXACT TIMING LOGIC: WHAT HAPPENS FIRST, SECOND, THIRD >>

If you want the most practical form of this whole section, use this exact order.

FIRST

  • stabilize everything required for Phase A

  • verify live split-source behavior

  • verify live Finnhub historical usability

  • freeze the serious dataset family

  • run market-only versus multimodal once, correctly

SECOND

  • analyze whether the event-state branch is stable, conditional, and interpretable

  • run only the core event-state ablations

  • do not widen scope yet

THIRD

  • run one narrow extension family at a time

  • derivative-family test

  • static metadata branch

  • maybe one stronger frozen embedding comparison

FOURTH

  • classify all findings into:

    • core supported

    • core conditional

    • extension supported

    • extension rejected

    • postponed

FIFTH

  • write the thesis around that classification, not around whichever idea sounded most elegant early on

<< 26.7 WHAT THE PROJECT SHOULD BE ABLE TO SAY AFTER EACH PHASE >>

After Phase A, the project should be able to say:

  • whether the core multimodal thesis is empirically alive

  • whether market-only learning is nontrivial

  • whether event-state adds anything under a fair benchmark

After Phase B, the project should be able to say:

  • what event-state design choices matter

  • whether usefulness is stable or conditional

  • which horizons and density conditions matter most

After Phase C, the project should be able to say:

  • whether the derivative family adds true incremental value or is redundant

  • whether static metadata helps enough to matter

  • which tempting extensions were not worth promoting

After Phase D, the thesis should be able to say:

  • what the project is truly about at its core

  • what it established honestly

  • what it rejected honestly

  • and what should come next without pretending that every interesting idea belongs in the main claim

<< 26.8 HARD CRITIQUE OF THE WRONG PATH FROM HERE >>

The wrong path from here would be:

  • change the universe repeatedly

  • test many target families at once

  • escalate derivative windows early

  • add richer fusion because it looks sophisticated

  • introduce company profile text before the static branch is even proven useful

  • call pilot results “main findings”

  • and then write the thesis as if all of this were one coherent experiment family

That would produce:

  • benchmark drift

  • interpretability collapse

  • weak attribution of gains

  • and a thesis that sounds ambitious but is scientifically soft

The repo itself is already warning against this path by emphasizing:

  • baseline-first development

  • split handling before labels

  • frozen intermediate artifacts before training

  • and no widening of scope before the previous stage has both code and tests.

<< 26.9 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

The actual staged research plan from here is very simple in principle:

  • First, prove the thesis core under frozen serious conditions.

  • Second, understand the event-state branch carefully.

  • Third, allow only a few controlled extensions.

  • Fourth, write the thesis around the truth that survives this process.

The derivative idea has a place, but that place is late, narrow, and comparative.
It should enter only after the main market-only versus event-state benchmark is already stable enough that an additional feature family can be judged fairly.

That is the sequence most consistent with the repo’s current state, the research design, the implementation roadmap, the execution flow, and the project’s own stated priorities.

<< 27. THE FINAL CLASSIFICATION MAP: WHAT IS CORE NOW, WHAT IS STRONG NEXT, WHAT IS EXTENSION, WHAT IS RISKY, AND WHAT SHOULD PROBABLY BE REJECTED >>

This section is the final staging map.
It is not a winner-picking memo.
It is a disciplined classification of what the restarted research should treat as:

  • core now

  • strong next-step candidate

  • extension if time allows

  • attractive but risky

  • probably not worth prioritizing

This classification is grounded in the current repo reality:

  • the project is already in late foundation / early experimentation

  • the main infrastructure is already implemented end to end

  • the remaining priorities are documentation hardening, richer reporting, selected extensions, and live external verification

  • the architecture is intentionally conservative and baseline-first

  • richer multimodal variants are explicitly later-stage work, not the current core

<< 27.1 CORE NOW >>

These are the things the project should treat as the true present core.
They are not optional.
They define what the thesis is really about right now.

  1. End-of-day, leakage-aware, multi-horizon excess-return forecasting

Why core now:

  • it is the project’s declared identity

  • it is the most defensible target framing

  • it avoids the methodological weakness of price-level prediction

  • it aligns with the implemented pipeline and evaluation logic

Hard judgment:
This is non-negotiable.
If you drift away from this, you are no longer doing the same project.

  1. Event-state framing instead of isolated-article effect framing

Why core now:

  • it is the conceptual center of the research

  • it is repeated consistently across README and research design

  • it is more defensible than pretending each article has a clean isolated price impact

Hard judgment:
This should remain the project’s main theoretical identity.
Do not downgrade it into just “some text branch.”

  1. Split-adjusted price discipline

Why core now:

  • raw OHLCV from Twelve Data appears unadjusted in important windows

  • the repository already built explicit local split handling because this is a scientific blocker

  • labels and features are not trustworthy without it

Hard judgment:
This is not a preprocessing detail.
It is part of the thesis validity boundary.

  1. Strict as-of-close article alignment

Why core now:

  • the repo already centralizes alignment rules

  • evaluation protocol depends on it

  • the event-state branch becomes scientifically weak if timing is fuzzy

Hard judgment:
This is also non-negotiable.

  1. Market-only baseline versus multimodal comparison

Why core now:

  • the current architecture, roadmap, and evaluation stack all support this directly

  • it is the minimal fair test of the main hypothesis

  • without this comparison the thesis has no proper anchor

Hard judgment:
This is the main empirical question.
Everything else is subordinate to it.

  1. Conservative market feature family

Why core now:

  • the README explicitly recommends conservative market features first

  • the current feature layer already implements them

  • they are benchmark-clean and interpretable

  • they reduce the risk of feature-bloat self-deception

Hard judgment:
This is the right base layer.
Do not replace it with a feature zoo.

  1. Frozen embeddings plus offline event-state construction

Why core now:

  • it is already implemented

  • it fits the project’s reproducibility and efficiency stance

  • it keeps the text pipeline interpretable and benchmarkable

Hard judgment:
For the thesis core, this is the correct default.
Not because it is the fanciest, but because it is the most defensible.

  1. Walk-forward plus purge and embargo evaluation

Why core now:

  • the evaluation protocol makes this central

  • the split and leakage layers already support it

  • it is essential for serious financial ML claims

Hard judgment:
Any result that bypasses this should not count as thesis-grade evidence.

<< 27.2 STRONG NEXT-STEP CANDIDATES >>

These are the best immediate next research targets after the core serious run.
They are strongly aligned with the project and likely worth doing.
But they are still one layer below the core itself.

  1. Event-state aggregation ablations

Includes:

  • simple mean

  • exponential decay

  • maybe linear decay

Why strong next:

  • directly tests the core event-state design

  • low architectural friction

  • easy to compare fairly

  • already anticipated by the research design

Judgment:
This is one of the best Phase B priorities.

  1. Lookback-window ablations

Includes:

  • 7d

  • 14d

  • 30d

Why strong next:

  • directly tied to the semantics of event persistence

  • directly relevant to multi-horizon forecasting

  • low-friction and benchmark-clean

Why strong next:
