  • helps explain conditional usefulness

  • often more informative than just chasing average metric deltas

  • already anticipated in the research design

Judgment:
This is one of the most thesis-valuable analyses you can do.

  1. Time-period stability analysis

Why strong next:

  • reveals whether the result is regime-fragile

  • supports or weakens the credibility of the main finding

  • fits the current evaluation philosophy cleanly

Judgment:
This is essential for honest interpretation.

  1. Dense embeddings versus coarse text baseline

Why strong next:

  • helps determine whether true semantic representation matters

  • tests whether the text branch is genuinely smart or just a soft proxy for volume/sentiment

  • already aligned with old hypothesis structure

Judgment:
Strong next-step, but only after the core benchmark is proven interpretable.

  1. Multi-horizon versus single-horizon comparison

Why strong next:

  • tests whether shared representation is helping

  • still close enough to the thesis core to be meaningful

  • easy to justify scientifically

Judgment:
Good Phase B candidate.

<< 27.3 EXTENSION IF TIME ALLOWS >>

These ideas are genuinely relevant and not bad.
But they should not define the current restarted project unless the core is already stable.

  1. Static company metadata branch

Includes:

  • sector

  • SIC

  • exchange

  • identity priors

Why extension:

  • useful

  • likely low leakage compared with dynamic profile text

  • repo support already exists for KB generation

  • but it is still less central than the market plus event-state question

Judgment:
Good extension.
Not core.

  1. Stronger reporting and evaluation polish

Includes:

  • richer tables

  • better figures

  • more polished confidence interval reporting

Why extension:

  • highly useful

  • already listed as a remaining priority

  • but not a substitute for empirical clarity

Judgment:
Important for thesis finish quality, but not the same as new science.

  1. One stronger frozen embedding model comparison

Why extension:

  • relevant

  • easy to justify after the core event-state claim is established

  • but not necessary before proving that event state helps at all

Judgment:
Good extension if compute and time permit.

  1. Controlled uncertainty-aware output variant

Why extension:

  • scientifically interesting

  • mentioned as optional direction in the repo documents

  • but secondary to proving the central predictive value first

Judgment:
Worth considering only after stable main results exist.

  1. Narrow derivative-family experiment

This is where your derivative proposal belongs.

Why extension:

  • not necessary to prove the main thesis

  • likely redundant with stronger standard market features unless proven otherwise

  • can still be tested fairly and usefully if kept narrow

Judgment:
Valid extension.
Not core.
Not early.

<< 27.4 ATTRACTIVE BUT RISKY >>

These directions are not necessarily bad.
But they have a high chance of harming benchmark cleanliness, inflating complexity, or consuming time without a proportional thesis return.

  1. Time-varying company profile branch

Why risky:

  • leakage-sensitive

  • timestamp discipline is difficult

  • easy to contaminate historical realism

  • the repo itself says not to do this too early

Judgment:
Attractive academically.
High risk operationally and methodologically.

  1. Attention-based event-state pooling

Why risky:

  • more expressive

  • but harder to benchmark fairly

  • easier to overfit

  • may not add enough over simple decay pooling to justify itself

Judgment:
Possible future direction, but only after simpler pooling is characterized fully.

  1. Richer multimodal fusion architectures

Includes:

  • deeper branch interactions

  • learned routing

  • more elaborate fusion heads

Why risky:

  • architecture inflation risk

  • gains become harder to attribute

  • repo explicitly places richer multimodal ablations after current results are stable

Judgment:
Interesting, but easy to misuse as sophistication theater.

  1. Derivative-family expansion beyond a narrow set

Includes:

  • many windows

  • many transforms

  • first and second order everywhere

Why risky:

  • strong window-shopping risk

  • high redundancy

  • can create many weakly motivated comparison degrees of freedom

  • easy to overfit to noise

Judgment:
A narrow derivative test is acceptable.
A large derivative program is risky and probably wasteful.

  1. Sector-heavy or regime-heavy tailored modeling before strong global baselines

Why risky:

  • may produce attractive localized wins

  • but can hide the fact that the general thesis core is not stable yet

  • smaller subgroup sample sizes weaken confidence

Judgment:
Do not let subgroup tailoring replace core benchmark strength.

<< 27.5 PROBABLY NOT WORTH PRIORITIZING >>

These are the directions that currently look least attractive relative to cost, thesis value, and benchmark cleanliness.

  1. End-to-end text fine-tuning right now

Why not worth prioritizing:

  • high compute burden

  • lower reproducibility

  • harder ablations

  • harder attribution of gains

  • explicitly listed as something not to do too early

Judgment:
Postpone strongly.

  1. Mixture-of-Experts or expert-routing as near-term thesis core

Why not worth prioritizing:

  • too much architecture before the core claim is proven

  • added interpretability and benchmark burden

  • very weak fit with current project maturity

Judgment:
Interesting later research topic, weak current priority.

  1. Graph or relation-aware market-text architectures right now

Why not worth prioritizing:

  • high friction

  • large data and design burden

  • easy to create impressive complexity without strong causal improvement

  • not aligned with the current repo’s immediate priorities

Judgment:
Too far from the current core.

  1. Full target zoo expansion before the main result is stable

Includes:

  • raw returns

  • excess returns

  • abnormal returns

  • direction

  • downside

  • quantiles

  • calibration-first outputs all together

Why not worth prioritizing:

  • problem-definition drift

  • comparability collapse

  • interpretability dilution

Judgment:
Pick a core target family and stay there first.

  1. Full 503-name live experiment as the first main thesis benchmark

Why not worth prioritizing:

  • provider quota pressure

  • longer debugging cycles

  • higher operational noise

  • execution flow already advises against jumping there too early

Judgment:
Use curated serious subsets first.

<< 27.6 WHAT SHOULD PROBABLY BE REJECTED UNLESS STRONG NEW EVIDENCE APPEARS >>

This section is intentionally harsh.

  1. Treating raw unadjusted OHLCV as acceptable for serious labels

Reason:

  • directly conflicts with project risk analysis

  • undermines target integrity

  • repo already built explicit split handling because this is not acceptable

Judgment:
Reject.

  1. Treating derivative elegance as sufficient justification

Reason:

  • mathematical elegance is not evidence

  • derivative-like transforms are highly likely to be redundant unless proven otherwise

  • the project should not preserve them just because they feel analytically neat

Judgment:
Reject that mindset.
Only keep derivatives if they survive fair comparison.

  1. Treating pilot outputs as final thesis results

Reason:

  • the repo itself warns against this

  • manual external verification remains pending

  • pilot systems are for validation, not overclaiming

Judgment:
Reject.

  1. Treating more modalities as automatically better science

Reason:

  • complexity can mask weak labels, weak alignment, or weak benchmarks

  • the repo’s philosophy is explicitly correctness first, sophistication later

Judgment:
Reject.

  1. Reframing the thesis around direct price prediction

Reason:

  • directly conflicts with the current research formulation

  • weaker academically

  • less stationary

  • easier to produce misleading-looking success

Judgment:
Reject.

<< 27.7 FINAL DECISION MAP IN COMPACT FORM >>

CORE NOW

  • EOD excess-return framing

  • event-state concept

  • split-adjusted price discipline

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • conservative market feature branch

  • market-only versus multimodal comparison

  • frozen embeddings plus offline event-state

  • walk-forward with purge and embargo

  • saved-prediction evaluation

STRONG NEXT-STEP CANDIDATES

  • event-state pooling ablations

  • lookback ablations

  • news-density heterogeneity

  • time-period stability

  • dense embeddings versus coarse text baseline

  • multi-horizon versus single-horizon comparison

EXTENSION IF TIME ALLOWS

  • static company metadata branch

  • richer evaluation/reporting polish

  • one stronger frozen embedding comparison

  • controlled uncertainty-aware outputs

  • narrow derivative-family experiment

ATTRACTIVE BUT RISKY

  • time-varying profile branch

  • attention pooling

  • richer fusion systems

  • broad derivative-family expansion

  • early subgroup-specialized modeling

PROBABLY NOT WORTH PRIORITIZING

  • end-to-end text fine-tuning now

  • MoE / expert routing now

  • graph-aware models now

  • target-zoo inflation

  • full 503-name live benchmark first

PROBABLY REJECT

  • raw unadjusted labels

  • derivative elegance as justification

  • pilot outputs as final evidence

  • complexity as a proxy for rigor

  • reversion to price-level prediction

<< 27.8 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

The cleanest summary is this:

The project’s real core is already clear.
It is not “all possible multimodal finance ideas.”
It is:
an end-of-day, leakage-aware, split-safe, event-state-driven, multi-horizon excess-return forecasting study with market-only versus multimodal comparison at the center.

Everything else should be staged around that truth.

Your derivative proposal is not nonsense, but it is not core.
At best, right now, it belongs in:

  • extension if time allows
    or

  • attractive but risky,
    depending on how narrowly and cleanly it is tested.

That is the hard-critical classification that best matches the current repo state, the current roadmap, the execution flow, and the research design.

<< 28. THE FINAL RESTART CONCLUSION: WHAT THE PROJECT SHOULD NOW BE ABOUT, WHAT MUST BE PRESERVED, WHAT SHOULD BE DISCARDED, AND WHAT THE MOST DANGEROUS NEXT MISTAKES WOULD BE >>

This is the final restart conclusion.

It is not a model-selection memo.
It is not a hype statement.
It is not a promise that every attractive idea deserves implementation.

It is the clearest possible answer to:

  • what this project really is now,

  • what its strongest intellectual core is,

  • what parts of its prior history deserve preservation,

  • what should be demoted or discarded,

  • and what mistakes would most likely damage the thesis from this point forward.

The repository is no longer a vague concept skeleton.
It is already a coherent first-pass end-to-end research system with implemented support for ingestion, split handling, text alignment, event-state construction, final panel assembly, market-only baselines, first multimodal training, and evaluation or ablation tooling. Its explicitly stated remaining priorities are documentation hardening, richer reporting, selected later extensions, and manual external verification rather than uncontrolled architecture growth.

<< 28.1 WHAT THE PROJECT SHOULD NOW BE ABOUT AT ITS CORE >>

The project should now be about exactly this:

An end-of-day, leakage-aware, split-safe, event-state-driven, multi-horizon excess-return forecasting study that tests whether aggregated recent company-news information adds incremental value beyond conservative market-only baselines.

That is the cleanest and most defensible core.
It is already supported by the current README, the research design, the current architecture overview, and the evaluation protocol. The repo explicitly defines itself as:

  • not a price-level prediction system,

  • not a trading bot,

  • not intraday or HFT,

  • but an end-of-day multimodal multi-horizon research system centered on event-state modeling and academically defensible forecasting.

This means the core thesis should not be framed as:

  • “build the smartest finance model possible”

  • or “test every multimodal finance idea”

  • or “invent novel features until metrics go up”

It should be framed as:

  • define a defensible forecasting task,

  • build the cleanest benchmark ladder,

  • test market-only versus event-state multimodal fairly,

  • characterize where multimodal value exists, if it exists,

  • and reject attractive ideas that do not survive disciplined comparison.

That is what the restart should be about.

<< 28.2 WHAT MUST BE PRESERVED FROM THE PRIOR PROJECT HISTORY >>

Several parts of the prior project history should absolutely be preserved, because they are not noise.
They are the strongest parts of the project’s evolution.

  1. The rejection of price-level prediction

This was correct.
The research design and README both make clear that direct price prediction is the wrong framing because it is non-stationary, methodologically weak, and too easy to misinterpret. The move toward return-based and especially excess-return-style targets was a genuine improvement in scientific maturity.

Preserve:

  • return-oriented framing

  • excess-return or abnormal-return preference

  • multi-horizon evaluation

  1. The move from isolated article impact to event-state modeling

This is one of the most important conceptual improvements in the whole project.
It is not just a stylistic choice.
It is the theory that makes the project coherent.

Preserve:

  • the claim that financial news arrives as overlapping narrative flow

  • the view that recent information should be represented as an evolving state

  • the refusal to pretend every article has one clean causal price effect

That conceptual basis is one of the project’s strongest academic assets.

  1. The baseline-first philosophy

The repo’s implementation order, architecture, roadmap, and evaluation materials all reinforce the right principle:
correctness and benchmark discipline come before sophistication.

Preserve:

  • market-only first

  • multimodal second

  • extensions only after core results stabilize

  1. The explicit split-handling emphasis

This should be preserved without compromise.
The project correctly recognized that unadjusted OHLCV would poison labels and benchmark validity.
The current design around explicit split-event sourcing and local back-adjustment is one of the most important scientific corrections made by the project.

Preserve:

  • raw versus adjusted separation

  • local adjustment traceability

  • split diagnostics

  • refusal to trust provider adjustment blindly

  1. The strict alignment and leakage-awareness culture

This is another strong asset.
The project already centralizes as-of-close logic, walk-forward splits, purge and embargo logic, and stored-prediction evaluation. That culture should remain central to the thesis identity, not treated as background engineering.

Preserve:

  • strict time ordering

  • strict article cutoff rules

  • purge and embargo

  • frozen datasets and saved-prediction comparisons

<< 28.3 WHAT SHOULD BE DISCARDED OR DEMOTED FROM THE PRIOR HISTORY >>

Some earlier instincts or possible future drifts should now be demoted or discarded.

  1. The idea that more architecture is automatically more scientific

Discard this.
The repository itself now embodies the opposite principle:
correctness first, sophistication later.

What to discard:

  • any impulse to equate deeper fusion, more branches, or trendier architectures with stronger research

  • any assumption that complexity is needed before the core question is even answered

  1. The idea that every useful-sounding modality belongs in the main thesis

Demote this.
Static metadata may help.
Dynamic profile text may help.
Raw mainstream news may help.
Graph relations may help.
But none of that belongs in the core before the current market plus event-state thesis is properly established.

What to demote:

  • time-varying company profile branch

  • raw descriptive external sources

  • advanced relation-aware structures

  • expert-routing ideas

  1. The temptation to let derivative-style features become a pseudo-core innovation

Demote this hard.
Your derivative idea is not automatically bad, but it is not currently central enough, benchmark-clean enough, or uniquely motivated enough to become part of the restart’s main identity.

What to demote:

  • first and second derivative families as a defining thesis contribution

  • large derivative-window grids

  • any belief that mathematical elegance alone makes the idea important

  1. The idea that pilot outputs can stand in for final results

Discard this.
The implementation roadmap explicitly says current pilot outputs should not be treated as final thesis evidence without live-data verification.

What to discard:

  • over-reading pilot wins

  • presenting systems-validation runs as empirical proof

  • letting convenience replace validation

<< 28.4 WHAT THE DERIVATIVE IDEA NOW REALLY IS >>

The derivative idea should now be understood in the most honest way possible.

It is:

  • not absurd

  • not obviously useless

  • not obviously core

  • not currently strong enough to define the project

  • worth testing only under narrow and controlled conditions after the core benchmark is stabilized

That is the right classification.

Why it is not core:

  • the main thesis question is market-only versus event-state multimodal value

  • derivative-like transforms mostly enrich the market branch rather than define the event-state thesis

  • many derivative-like effects are already partially captured by simpler and more standard feature families such as returns, momentum, rolling slope, volatility, range, and volume surprise

  • broad derivative expansion creates large benchmark degrees of freedom and high window-shopping risk

Why it is not nonsense:

  • a narrow derivative-like family might capture local change-of-motion information that simple returns miss

  • smoothed slope-like transforms may be useful for certain horizons

  • a controlled appendix experiment could test this fairly

The right conclusion is therefore:

Preserve the derivative idea only as a late, narrow, comparative experiment.
Discard any urge to make it the restart’s defining contribution.

That is the hard-critical position most consistent with the rest of the project.

<< 28.5 WHAT THE MOST DANGEROUS NEXT MISTAKES WOULD BE >>

These are the mistakes most likely to damage the thesis now.

  1. Mistaking implementation completeness for scientific validity

The repo is already impressively broad.
But a wide implemented pipeline does not itself prove forecasting validity.
A complete system can still be testing the wrong task, the wrong labels, or the wrong benchmark comparisons.

Danger:

  • writing the thesis as if system breadth equals scientific success

  1. Letting benchmark drift happen while calling everything “the same experiment”

This is probably one of the biggest practical threats now.

If you keep changing:

  • universe

  • target family

  • split source

  • event-state default

  • text variant

  • fold policy

  • benchmark definition

then you are not running one benchmark family anymore.
You are moving the goalposts.

Danger:

  • losing comparability while still speaking as if the results were directly comparable

  1. Using attractive extensions to avoid resolving the core question

This is another major danger.
When a core result is ambiguous, many projects escape into:

  • richer models

  • more features

  • more modalities

  • more subgroups

  • more custom targets

That usually makes the science weaker, not stronger.

Danger:

  • architecture inflation as avoidance behavior

  1. Underestimating the importance of conditional results

If multimodal value appears mainly in high-news-density periods or on certain horizons, that is not a weak result.
The dangerous mistake would be to hide it because it is not universal.

Danger:

  • throwing away the most believable result because it is not grand enough

  1. Overstating noisy gains

This is perhaps the most classic failure mode.
A small average gain that is fold-unstable, subgroup-dependent, or statistically weak should not be turned into a headline claim.

Danger:

  • rhetorical inflation of fragile signal

  1. Treating manual provider verification as optional

The roadmap explicitly lists live provider behavior, split-source reality, Finnhub historical completeness, and runtime realism as remaining priorities.

Danger:

  • basing thesis claims on assumptions about live data coverage or provider semantics that were never actually verified

  1. Reintroducing leakage through convenience shortcuts

The project has already done substantial work to encode strict alignment and time-safe evaluation. That can still be damaged later through careless shortcuts:

  • incorrect scaler fitting

  • fuzzy article cutoff logic

  • profile features using future knowledge

  • improper split windows

  • hidden notebook-side preprocessing

Danger:

  • subtle leakage hiding inside a seemingly mature system

<< 28.6 WHAT SHOULD DEFINITELY NOT BE DONE NEXT >>

The following things should definitely not be done next.

Do not:

  • make the derivative family the next main research axis

  • add end-to-end text fine-tuning now

  • add time-varying company profile text now

  • jump to full-scale live universe runs as the first serious thesis benchmark

  • change targets repeatedly to rescue metrics

  • blur pilot validation and final evidence

  • add graph or expert-routing complexity before proving the core thesis clearly

  • weaken split handling or alignment discipline in exchange for convenience

Each of these would increase complexity faster than understanding.

<< 28.7 WHAT SHOULD BE STABILIZED BEFORE ANY NEW IMPLEMENTATION PUSH >>

Before any major new implementation push, the project should stabilize the following:

  • one frozen serious universe definition

  • one frozen split-source and adjusted-price policy

  • one frozen article text variant

  • one frozen embedding backend for the thesis core

  • one frozen default event-state design

  • one frozen target family

  • one frozen fold policy

  • one frozen reporting packet

  • one verified provider-reality checklist

This stabilization logic is already strongly supported by the current README, data layout, evaluation protocol, execution flow, and implementation roadmap. The system is designed around raw/interim/final separation, manifests, stored-prediction evaluation, and controlled progression rather than informal experimentation drift.

<< 28.8 THE FINAL RESTART VERDICT >>

The final restart verdict is this:

The project should now be about a disciplined test of whether event-state representations from aligned recent company news provide incremental multi-horizon predictive value beyond conservative market-only baselines under strict end-of-day, split-safe, and leakage-aware conditions.

That is the project.

Not:

  • a generic multimodal finance sandbox

  • a feature-explosion project

  • a derivative-theory project

  • a race toward the most complex architecture

The parts that should be preserved are:

  • return-based framing

  • event-state conceptual identity

  • split-safe price discipline

  • strict as-of-close alignment

  • baseline-first experimental design

  • walk-forward plus purge and embargo evaluation

  • frozen intermediate artifacts and saved-prediction comparison

The parts that should be demoted or discarded are:

  • price-level ambitions

  • complexity as a substitute for rigor

  • derivative elegance as sufficient justification

  • premature expansion into extra branches and advanced architectures

  • any attempt to treat pilot behavior as final proof

The most dangerous next mistakes are:

  • benchmark drift

  • architecture inflation

  • overclaiming weak gains

  • skipping provider verification

  • and letting attractive extensions distract from the core empirical question

The strongest unresolved theoretical questions are now narrower and better defined:

  • Does market-only learning show stable out-of-sample value under the final serious benchmark family?

  • Does event-state information add robust value, conditional value, or no value?

  • Which event-state design choices matter most?

  • How much of any observed gain is stable across time and news-density conditions?

  • Does a narrow derivative-like feature family survive fair comparison, or is it just false sophistication?

That is exactly where the restart should leave the project:
clearer, narrower, harder, and more scientifically honest than before.

This section turns the whole restart into one consolidated operational checklist.

  • the project is already late foundation / early experimentation,

  • and the officially stated remaining priorities are documentation hardening, reporting polish, selected extensions, and manual external verification.

So the checklist below is not for building the repo from zero.
It is for restarting the research correctly on top of the implemented system.

<< 29.1 MASTER RULE BEFORE ANY NEW THESIS CLAIM >>

Before any new thesis claim is made, all of the following must be true:

  • the benchmark family is frozen

  • the target family is frozen

  • the universe definition is frozen

  • the split-handling policy is frozen

  • the text variant is frozen

  • the event-state default is frozen

  • the fold protocol is frozen

  • the run outputs are saved and reproducible

  • live provider assumptions used in the run have been manually verified

If any of those are still moving, then the project is still in benchmark-construction mode, not thesis-evidence mode.

This requirement is fully aligned with the repo’s current data-layout, evaluation, execution-flow, and roadmap documents, which all emphasize frozen datasets, manifests, saved predictions, strict temporal evaluation, and explicit rebuild traceability.

<< 29.2 CHECKLIST A — FREEZE THE THESIS CORE >>

Complete this checklist first.

A1. Freeze project identity

Confirm that the project is still defined as:

  • end-of-day

  • multimodal

  • multi-horizon

  • event-state driven

  • return-oriented rather than price-level oriented

  • leakage-aware

  • academically defensible rather than trading-bot oriented

If any new idea pushes the project outside that identity, stop and classify it as a separate extension, not as a quiet core change.

A2. Freeze the main research question

Freeze the main question as:

Does an aggregated event-state representation from aligned recent company news add incremental value beyond market-only baselines for multi-horizon excess-return prediction?

Do not let derivative features, profile branches, or richer fusion replace this question before it is answered once cleanly.

A3. Freeze the primary target family

Use one primary family only:

  • forward excess return by horizon

Keep direction and downside as secondary or auxiliary outputs, not as silent replacements for the main problem definition. The current project materials strongly support excess-return style targets as the main academically defensible choice.

A4. Freeze the primary horizons

Use only the serious core first:

  • 1d

  • 5d

  • 20d

Treat 60d as optional later unless the serious benchmark family is already stable.

A5. Freeze the default market feature family

Keep it conservative:

  • simple returns

  • log returns

  • rolling volatility

  • rolling momentum

  • intraday range proxies

  • volume ratios or surprises

  • benchmark-relative features

Do not widen this into a feature zoo before the first serious benchmark run.

A6. Freeze the default event-state design

Use one default only:

  • frozen text encoder

  • one chosen text variant

  • fixed lookback

  • fixed decay rule

  • fixed no-news handling

The current repo and research design both support this conservative event-state-first approach.

<< 29.3 CHECKLIST B — FREEZE THE DATA REALITY >>

This is where many financial ML projects quietly fail.

B1. Freeze the universe file

Choose one:

  • curated 30

  • curated 50

  • curated 100

Do not use a moving universe during the core thesis run.
Do not jump to all 503 names first. The execution flow already explicitly warns against that.

B2. Freeze the benchmark ticker or benchmark family

Use one benchmark reference consistently.
Do not alternate benchmark definitions across comparisons unless that is declared a separate benchmark family.

B3. Freeze split-event sourcing policy

You must decide exactly what split-event source is being trusted for the serious run:

  • audited Twelve Data split access

  • audited secondary provider

  • audited local import

The repo already treats split handling as a first-class scientific boundary, not a minor preprocessing detail.

B4. Freeze raw versus adjusted price separation

Confirm that:

  • adjusted price history is written separately

  • final labels use adjusted prices

  • split-adjustment diagnostics are recorded

B5. Freeze the article text policy

Choose exactly one:

  • headline only
    or

  • headline plus summary

Then keep it fixed for the core benchmark family.

  • fallback text-hash logic

  • stable timestamp normalization

  • stable as-of-close mapping

Confirm that the final dataset version writes:

  • schema version

  • dataset version

  • source tables

  • creation timestamp

  • traceable manifests

This is explicitly required by the current data-layout philosophy.

C1. Verify Twelve Data raw-history behavior on known split windows

At minimum manually verify:

  • AAPL 2020-08-31

  • TSLA 2020-08-31

  • NVDA 2021-07-20

C2. Verify actual split-event coverage under the chosen source policy

Do not assume the fallback source is perfect.
Check real coverage on a small serious subset.

C3. Verify Finnhub historical usability for the exact date range you want

Do not mistake empty article windows for a code failure or for usable coverage.
The execution flow explicitly warns about this.

C4. Verify dot-ticker behavior end to end

At minimum:

  • BRK.B

  • BF.B

C5. Verify the benchmark series is present and aligned

No serious excess-return work should proceed if the benchmark branch is incomplete or misaligned.

Confirm that no-news dates are handled exactly as expected and not silently dropped.

<< 29.5 CHECKLIST D — RUN THE FIRST SERIOUS THESIS WAVE >>

This is the first true research wave.

D1. Build the frozen serious dataset family

Required outputs:

  • adjusted prices

  • canonical news articles

  • embeddings

  • event states

  • final modeling panel

  • dataset manifest

D2. Run the baseline ladder

At minimum:

  • constant baseline

  • ridge or elastic net

  • one official market-only neural baseline if retained as core benchmark

D3. Run the first multimodal comparison

At minimum:

  • market-only
    versus

  • market plus event-state

D4. Evaluate using stored predictions against frozen labels

Do not rely on notebook-state evaluation.
The architecture and evaluation documents explicitly require saved-prediction evaluation against frozen datasets.

D5. Produce only the core result packet

Required:

  • fold summary

  • horizon summary

  • paired comparison summary

  • density subgroup summary

  • time-period stability summary

D6. Classify the outcome honestly

Classify the result as one of:

  • robust multimodal improvement

  • conditional multimodal improvement

  • no reliable multimodal improvement

  • weak task learnability overall

Do not widen scope until this classification is written down.

<< 29.6 CHECKLIST E — ONLY AFTER THAT, RUN THE SECOND WAVE >>

Do not start this section if the first serious wave is still ambiguous because of moving data or unstable execution.

E1. Event-state pooling ablation

Compare:

  • simple mean

  • exponential decay

  • maybe one additional simple variant only

E2. Lookback ablation

Keep it small:

  • 7d

  • 14d

  • 30d

E3. Representation ablation

Compare:

  • dense semantics

  • one coarser or weaker text representation only if already supported

E4. Heterogeneity analysis

Prioritize:

  • news-density slices

  • horizon slices

  • time-period stability

E5. Keep everything else fixed

Do not change:

  • universe

  • benchmark

  • split source

  • target family

  • text variant

  • fold policy

Otherwise this is no longer the second wave of the same benchmark family.

<< 29.7 CHECKLIST F — ONLY THEN ALLOW EXTENSIONS >>

This is where controlled late-stage additions belong.

F1. Narrow derivative-family challenge test

Only after the core benchmark family is stable.

Allowed:

  • first-order normalized transforms

  • rolling slope-like features

  • possibly one small second-order family

  • very small window set

Not allowed:

  • wide derivative grids

  • dozens of windows

  • redefining the thesis around derivatives

F2. Static company metadata branch

Allowed only after the market plus event-state question is already interpretable.

F3. One stronger frozen embedding comparison

Useful, but not before proving the core event-state branch has value at all.

F4. Optional uncertainty-aware output branch

Only if the core predictive setup already has stable evidence.

F5. Richer multimodal fusion

Only if the simpler multimodal result is already stable, reproducible, and worth refining.

<< 29.8 CHECKLIST G — RED FLAGS THAT SHOULD FORCE A STOP >>

Stop and re-evaluate if any of the following happens:

  • you change the universe mid-comparison

  • you change the split source mid-comparison

  • you change the target family mid-comparison

  • you change the text variant mid-comparison

  • you realize provider coverage assumptions were wrong

  • you cannot reproduce saved-prediction metrics from disk

  • event-state coverage is silently sparse or broken

  • labels were built from raw rather than adjusted prices

  • fold logic changed after results were already viewed

  • derivative experiments begin outnumbering core benchmark experiments

Any of these means the current comparison is no longer clean enough to support a serious thesis claim.

<< 29.9 CHECKLIST H — WHAT THE THESIS SHOULD BE ABLE TO SAY BEFORE WRITING STARTS >>

Before serious thesis writing begins, the project should be able to state clearly:

  • what the final frozen benchmark family was

  • what the primary target family was

  • what the serious universe was

  • what split source was used

  • what text variant and embedding backend were used

  • what the default event-state design was

  • what the baseline ladder was

  • whether multimodal value was robust, conditional, absent, or inconclusive

  • whether the derivative family was retained, demoted, or rejected

  • what was postponed and why

If any of those are still unclear, the project is not ready for final thesis writing.

<< 29.10 CHECKLIST I — FINAL RESEARCH DISCIPLINE RULES >>

Use these as permanent rules from now on.

Rule 1

  • Do not confuse more data with more signal.

Rule 2

  • Do not confuse more architecture with more science.

Rule 3

  • Do not treat derivatives as valuable because they look mathematically elegant.

Rule 4

  • Do not let benchmark drift hide behind the phrase “same experiment.”

Rule 5

  • Do not trade alignment rigor for convenience.

Rule 6

  • Do not treat pilot outputs as thesis-grade proof.

Rule 7

  • Do not let extension work answer a different question while pretending it answered the original one.

Rule 8

  • Do not write the thesis around the most interesting idea.

  • Write it around the strongest surviving evidence.

These rules are consistent with the repo’s current architecture boundaries, evaluation protocol, execution plan, and implementation roadmap.

<< 29.11 MASTER COMPACT VERSION >>

If everything above had to be compressed into one short operational sequence, it would be this:

  1. Freeze the task.

  2. Freeze the data reality.

  3. Verify provider reality manually.

  4. Run one serious market-only versus event-state benchmark family.

  5. Classify the result honestly.

  6. Only then run controlled event-state ablations.

  7. Only then allow narrow extensions.

  8. Keep derivatives late, narrow, and comparative.

  9. Write the thesis around the evidence that survives.

  10. Reject anything that gained importance only because it sounded sophisticated.

<< 29.12 DIRECT CONCLUSION FOR THIS CONTINUATION >>

The restart is now mature enough that the biggest risk is no longer lack of structure.

The biggest risk is losing discipline.

You now have:

  • a clear project identity,

  • a coherent implemented system,

  • a credible benchmark philosophy,

  • a viable serious-run path,

  • and a clear staging logic for extensions.

So the consolidated master sequencing checklist is simple in spirit:

Freeze first.
Verify second.
Benchmark third.
Interpret fourth.
Extend last.

That is the cleanest possible operational rule for the restarted research, and it is fully consistent with the repo’s current README, architecture, data layout, evaluation protocol, execution flow, guidebook, and roadmap.

Its purpose is not to add new ideas.

an end-of-day, leakage-aware, split-safe, multimodal, multi-horizon financial forecasting thesis project centered on whether an aggregated recent-news event state provides incremental value beyond conservative market-only baselines for forward excess-return prediction.

That statement is the strongest available compression of the README identity, the research design problem formulation, the architecture boundaries, and the evaluation protocol. It preserves the project’s central conceptual commitments:

  • not price-level prediction,

  • not intraday prediction,

  • not HFT,

  • not isolated article-effect modeling,

  • but event-state forecasting under strict temporal discipline.

<< 30.2 THE TRUE CORE OF THE RESTART >>

The restart should be understood as protecting five things above all else.

First:
the project must preserve return-oriented task design rather than slipping back toward raw future price prediction. Both the README and the research design explicitly reject price-level framing as methodologically weak for this thesis context.

Second:
the project must preserve the event-state concept rather than collapsing into isolated article sentiment logic. This is not just a modeling choice. It is the main theoretical lens through which the project explains overlapping narratives, noisy reactions, and temporally evolving information.

Third:
the project must preserve split-safe label construction. The repo’s own materials repeatedly treat corporate-action handling as a scientific validity issue rather than a preprocessing afterthought. Raw unadjusted OHLCV is not safe for serious label construction unless explicitly mitigated.

Fourth:
the project must preserve strict as-of-close temporal alignment, walk-forward chronology, and purge or embargo discipline. The evaluation protocol and architecture boundaries already define these as central rules, not optional implementation details.

Fifth:
the project must preserve baseline-first thinking. The repository has already been structured so that correctness, reproducibility, and comparability come before model sophistication. That sequencing should not be reversed now that the codebase is broad enough to tempt richer experiments.

<< 30.3 WHAT THE RESTART HAS NOW MADE CLEAR ABOUT THE DERIVATIVE IDEA >>

Your derivative idea has now been placed in the correct conceptual location.

It is not nonsense.
It is not an obvious core innovation.
It is not strong enough to define the thesis.
It is not worthless either.

The hard-critical conclusion is:

  • derivatives should not define the restart

  • derivatives should not be introduced before the first serious benchmark family is frozen

  • derivatives should only be tested as a narrow extension against stronger standard market-feature alternatives

  • derivatives should be kept only if they show incremental value beyond conservative baseline market features under fair comparison

Why this conclusion holds:

  • the central research question is still market-only versus event-state multimodal value

  • derivative features primarily enrich the market branch, not the event-state concept

  • many derivative-like transforms overlap heavily with simpler and more standard features such as returns, momentum, rolling slope, volatility, range, and volume surprise

  • broad derivative grids create dangerous benchmark degrees of freedom and make window shopping too easy

It does not survive as the restart’s main identity.

What should be inherited:

  • the move away from price-level framing

  • the move toward event-state theory

  • the insistence on leakage awareness

  • the explicit split-handling correction

  • the layered raw/interim/final data philosophy

  • the baseline-first implementation order

  • the commitment to saved predictions, manifests, and frozen dataset logic

What should not be inherited:
